title: Balance as a team: how eyes, ears and feet keep you upright, and the senses other animals have

summary.text: Stand on one foot with your eyes shut on a folded blanket, and you wobble far more than on the bare floor with your eyes open. Your ears are the same both times, so what changed? Balance is not one sense in one place. Your eyes, your inner ears and the stretch sensors in your legs each give a rough answer, and your brain mixes them. Your child tests this by taking one sense away at a time. They read a page while shaking their head, and then while the page is shaken. They find that a fingertip pressing more lightly than the weight of a tomato can steady a whole body. Then the unit looks at how we sense warmth, pain and the heartbeat, and at flies that steer with tiny clubs, snakes that sense heat, and fish that carry ear stones.
summary.art: A child standing on one foot on a folded blanket with her eyes shut and a grown-up close beside her, with three small labelled arrows going to her head from her eyes, her ears and her feet.

intro.hook: You sit in a train at the station. The train on the next track starts to move slowly. For a moment you feel your own train sliding backwards, though nothing under you has moved. Who fooled you: your eyes or your body?
intro.text: Your eyes said you were moving. Your inner ears and the seat said you were still. For a second your brain believed your eyes, and then it checked the other signals and put things right. This shows that balance is a team of senses that can disagree. In this unit you take one member of the team away and see what happens. You test how your eyes stay steady when your head shakes. You find out how a fingertip can steady you, how the skin senses warmth and cold, why pain changes with attention, and how a fly keeps steady with two tiny clubs.
intro.art: Two trains side by side at a platform, with a girl at a window looking at the other train, and a thought bubble showing her train sliding backwards.

outcomes: I can name the three sources of information my brain uses for balance, and say what each one tells me.
I can explain, using the Balance Team test, why taking one sense away makes me wobble more but does not make me fall.
I can explain how my inner ears keep my eyes steady when my head moves, using the Shake the Head or Shake the Page test as evidence.
I can explain why a moving train beside me can make me feel I am moving, and how this links to feeling sick in a car.
I can explain how my skin senses warmth and cold with separate gates, and how my body keeps its temperature steady with a sensing loop.
I can explain why there are two kinds of pain, and why pain can change when I pay attention to something else.
I can describe a sense that another animal has, say what problem the sense solves, and say how the sense is like one I have.
I can plan a fair test that changes one thing at a time, give a guess with a reason, and use what I found to explain the result.

terms.meaning: The three sources of information your brain mixes to know whether you are upright. They are your eyes, your inner ears, and the sensors in the skin, muscles and joints of your legs and feet.
terms.example: On a dark staircase your eyes help little, so your ears and feet do more of the work.
terms.art: A girl on a dark staircase with three glowing arrows from her eyes, ears and feet going up into her head.

terms.meaning: The balance organs deep inside each inner ear. They have three liquid-filled canals that feel turning, and two pouches of ear crystals that feel tilting and speeding up.
terms.example: When a lift starts to go up, your vestibular system feels it, even with the doors shut.
terms.art: A cut-away of an ear showing three loops and two small pouches next to a spiral snail shell for hearing.

terms.meaning: One of three liquid-filled loops in each inner ear. When your head turns, the liquid lags behind and bends tiny hairs, and the hairs send signals to your brain.
terms.example: Shaking your head to say no moves the liquid in one canal.
terms.art: A loop of tube with a small bump at its base, shaded blue, with an arrow showing the liquid lagging behind a turn.

terms.meaning: Tiny crystals of calcium carbonate, the same stuff as chalk, resting on jelly over hair cells in the inner ear. Gravity pulls on them, so they tell you which way is down. Scientists call them otoliths.
terms.example: When you tilt your head, the crystals slide a little and bend the hairs under them.
terms.art: A magnified layer of jelly with white crystals on top and hairs poking up from below, tilted to one side.

terms.meaning: A very quick movement of your eyes in the opposite direction to your head turn, which keeps what you are looking at steady. It starts in the inner ear. Scientists call it the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
terms.example: You can read a sign while your head bobs on a bumpy auto ride because of this reflex.
terms.art: A head turning left while two eyes turn right, with a small arrow from the ear to the eye muscles.

terms.meaning: Fast flicking of the eyes from side to side that happens by itself. It happens after spinning, because the brain thinks the head is still turning.
terms.example: A grown-up can see your eyes flick for a few seconds after you stop spinning.
terms.art: A close-up of two eyes with small arrows beside them, flicking left and then slowly drifting right.

terms.meaning: The stretch and pressure sensors in your skin, muscles, tendons and joints. They tell your brain how your body parts are placed and what the ground feels like. Scientists call this the somatosensory system.
terms.example: The soles of your feet tell you if the floor is hard, soft or tilted.
terms.art: A pair of bare feet on a floor, with tiny glowing dots in the soles, the ankles and the calf muscles.

terms.meaning: The small, constant movements of a standing body, forwards, backwards and sideways, as the body keeps itself upright. Everyone sways, even when they feel perfectly still.
terms.example: If you hold a cup of water while standing, the surface trembles a little because you sway.
terms.art: A standing girl drawn three times in a row, each slightly leaning in a different direction, with a straight dotted line behind her.

terms.meaning: Listening more to the senses that are working well and less to the ones that are not. The brain does this without you choosing.
terms.example: In a dark room your brain listens more to your feet and ears.
terms.art: A set of three volume dials labelled eyes, ears and feet, with the eyes dial turned down and the other two turned up.

terms.meaning: A moment when two of your senses send messages that do not match, so the brain does not know which to believe.
terms.example: When you read in a bus, your eyes say you are still and your ears say you are moving.
terms.art: A child reading in a bus with one thought bubble saying still, another saying moving, and a question mark between them.

terms.meaning: The feeling that you are moving when only the world you see is moving.
terms.example: When the train beside you pulls out, you may feel your own train slide the other way.
terms.art: A girl at a train window looking at the next train moving away, her own train drawn still, with a faint arrow in her chest.

terms.meaning: Resting one fingertip on something still, pressing so lightly that it could not hold you up. Even so, it makes you steadier.
terms.example: Resting one fingertip on a wall helps you stand in the dark.
terms.art: A fingertip resting on a wall with a tiny arrow for force and a large arrow for the weight of the whole child beside it.

terms.meaning: A nerve ending that reacts to warmth or cold. Warm ones and cold ones are different, and sit in different places.
terms.example: Cold thermoreceptors in your lips fire when you sip cold water.
terms.art: A zoomed-in drawing of skin with a blue nerve ending near the top and a red nerve ending beside it.

terms.meaning: A tiny gate in the wall of a nerve cell. When a gate opens, charged particles rush in and the nerve sends a signal. Some gates open when it is warm, some when it is cool, some for chilli or mint.
terms.example: The gate that opens for chilli is the same gate that opens when something is too hot.
terms.art: A nerve cell wall drawn as a wall with a small gate, closed on the left and open on the right with dots flowing through.

terms.meaning: The heat of the deep parts of your body. It is kept close to 37 degrees Celsius, whether the day is hot or cold.
terms.example: A thermometer under your tongue reads close to your core temperature.
terms.art: A body outline with a warm glowing centre and cooler edges, and a thermometer reading about 37.

terms.meaning: A loop in which a sensor checks something, and then the body acts to bring it back to the level it should be. The result is checked again, and again.
terms.example: You get too warm, you sweat, you cool down, and then you stop sweating.
terms.art: A circle of four arrows: sense, compare, act, check, with a sweating child at the centre.

terms.meaning: Two kinds of pain signal. The fast one is sharp and tells you where you were hurt. The slow one is dull and throbbing and lasts longer.
terms.example: When you stub your toe, you feel a sharp jab first, and then a throb a moment later.
terms.art: A stubbed toe with two arrows going up the leg, a short fast one labelled sharp and a long slow one labelled throb.

terms.meaning: The senses that look inward. They tell you about your heartbeat, breathing, hunger, thirst and how full you are.
terms.example: You can feel your heart pounding after you run.
terms.art: A child with a hand on her chest and faint lines from her heart and stomach up to her head.

terms.meaning: A tiny club-shaped stalk behind each wing of a fly or a mosquito. It swings up and down as the wings beat, and it senses when the body turns.
terms.example: A housefly that has lost her halteres cannot fly in a straight line.
terms.art: A fly seen from above with a tiny arrow pointing at the two small knobbed stalks behind her wings.

terms.meaning: A small hollow on the face of some snakes, covered by a thin skin that senses warmth from a distance. It lets the snake sense the heat of a warm animal in the dark.
terms.example: A python has a row of heat pits along her lips.
terms.art: The head of a python seen from the side, with a row of small pits along the lip and a warm mouse glowing red nearby.

terms.meaning: A small hard stone in a fish's inner ear. It rests on sensing hairs and helps the fish know which way is up and when she is moving. It grows a thin new layer every day.
terms.example: Scientists count the layers in a fish's ear stone to learn how old she is.
terms.art: A small white ear stone drawn large, with thin rings like a tree trunk, and a rohu fish swimming beside the stone.

explanations.concept: Balance is a team of three
explanations.definition: Your brain knows whether you are upright by mixing three sources: your eyes, your inner ears, and the sensors in your skin, muscles and joints.
explanations.description: Each source tells the brain something different. Your eyes show where the horizon, the walls and the floor are. Your inner ears feel your head turn, tilt and speed up. The sensors in your feet and legs feel the ground under you and how your joints are bent. None of the three is perfect. Eyes do not work in the dark. Inner ears cannot tell a steady lift from standing still. Feet are poor guides on sand or a soft mattress. So the brain compares all three, many times each second, and makes small corrections to your muscles. A doctor called Moritz Romberg, in the 1840s, noticed that some patients stood steadily with their eyes open, but swayed or fell when they shut their eyes. Doctors still use his test today.
examples: Walking down a dark staircase in a power cut uses your ears and feet more, because your eyes help very little.
Standing in a moving bus with your eyes shut is harder than with your eyes open, because one member of the team is missing.
Walking on a sandy beach feels more tiring than on a road, because the soft sand makes the foot sensors less sure.
explanations.art: A girl standing upright with three labelled lines from her eyes, her inner ears and her feet joining at her brain, and a fourth line going down to her leg muscles.
explanations.context: This card explains why balance is not one sense in one place, but three sources of information that the brain mixes.

explanations.concept: What happens when one member of the team is taken away
explanations.definition: When one source of balance information is missing or unreliable, the brain relies more on the other two. This is called reweighting. You wobble more, but you usually do not fall.
explanations.description: In the 1970s and 1980s, the researcher Lewis Nashner and others built floors that tilted with the person's own sway, and rooms whose walls moved with the person's sway. These tricks made one source of information useless, because it no longer matched the real tilt of the body. Healthy people wobbled more at first. Then, after a few tries, they began to rely on the other sources, and they steadied again. A person who shuts their eyes on a soft surface loses two sources at once, and has only the ears left. That is the hardest case, and most people wobble a great deal. People who have lost the use of their inner ears can still stand quite well on a hard floor with their eyes open. They often fall in the dark, or on soft ground. This shows that no single member of the team holds you up alone. In a space station there is no down, so the ear crystals float on their jelly and the ears give odd messages. Many astronauts feel sick at first, until the brain adjusts.
examples: With your eyes shut on a firm floor, you wobble a little more, but you can stand.
On a folded blanket with your eyes open, your eyes make up for the feet.
On a folded blanket with your eyes shut, only your ears are left, and most people wobble a lot.
explanations.art: Four small pictures of a child standing: eyes open on floor, eyes shut on floor, eyes open on blanket, eyes shut on blanket, with the wobble drawn as a bigger and bigger shake.
explanations.context: This card explains the result of the Balance Team test, where you take one sense away at a time.

explanations.concept: The head-turn reflex: how your eyes stay on target
explanations.definition: When your head turns, the canals in your inner ear send a signal that moves your eyes the opposite way by almost the same amount, so the picture on your eye stays steady. It is called the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
explanations.description: When you film a video while walking, the picture jerks with every step. Your own eyes would do the same if nothing steadied them. The canals feel the head turn, and within about a hundredth of a second they send a signal to the eye muscles. The eyes swing the opposite way, so the thing you are looking at stays still on your eye. This is faster than anything you could do on purpose. When you follow a moving page with your eyes on purpose, the tracking is much slower, and it cannot keep up with a quick shake. That is why you can read while you shake your head, and cannot read while the page shakes. The same reflex explains why your eyes flick after spinning. The liquid in the canals keeps swirling after you stop, and it keeps telling the eyes to move.
examples: You can read a signboard while your head bobs on a bumpy bus ride.
A dancer who spins can whip her head round and still keep her eyes on one spot.
After spinning, you cannot read a page, because your eyes are flicking by themselves.
explanations.art: A head turning to the left with the eyes turning to the right and a dotted line showing the eyes staying locked on a distant lamp.
explanations.context: This card explains the result of the Shake the Head or Shake the Page test.

explanations.concept: Moving rooms and moving trains: when the senses disagree
explanations.definition: If your eyes say you are moving but your ears and feet say you are still, the brain may believe your eyes. This is called vection. It is one kind of sensory conflict.
explanations.description: In 1974, the researchers David Lee and Eric Aronson built a room with a floor that stayed still and walls and a ceiling that could slide forwards and backwards. Toddlers who stood in this room swayed or fell when the walls moved, though the floor did not. Their eyes told them the room was moving, and they corrected for it. The train on the next track does the same to you. Sensory conflict also seems to be involved in feeling sick in a car or on a boat. If you read in a car, your eyes say you are still, while your ears feel every turn and bump. The brain does not know whom to believe. Looking out of the window, at the horizon, makes the messages agree again. Scientists still argue about the exact cause of travel sickness, so this is the best-known idea, not the last word.
examples: The train beside yours pulls out, and you feel as if you are sliding backwards.
A cinema ride that tilts the picture makes you lean, though your seat is still.
Looking at the road ahead through the front window can ease sickness in a car.
explanations.art: A toddler standing in a room whose walls are drawn sliding forward, with the toddler leaning backwards and the floor drawn firm and still.
explanations.context: This card explains the train illusion, and how disagreement between senses can make you feel moved or sick.

explanations.concept: A fingertip that steadies a whole body
explanations.definition: Resting one fingertip on a still object, with a force of less than about 1 newton (about the weight of a small tomato), makes people sway less, even with their eyes shut. The touch gives the brain a fourth source of information.
explanations.description: In 1994, two researchers, John Jeka and James Lackner, asked people to stand in a difficult pose, with their feet in a line, one in front of the other. They found that a fingertip resting on a rail steadied people a great deal, even when the force of the touch was less than 1 newton. One newton is about the weight of a small tomato. That is far too small to hold up a standing person. So the touch does not work as a prop. It works as a sense. A still wall under the fingertip tells the brain exactly how the body is moving compared with the room. Studies since then have reported the same in older people, and a walking stick held lightly can help in the same way. A stick that you lean on is a support. A stick that you only touch is a sensor.
examples: Resting one fingertip on a wall helps you stand on one foot with your eyes shut.
A person who walks with a stick touches the ground lightly, as a cat uses her whiskers.
Holding the rail on a moving bus helps even when you hardly press on it.
explanations.art: A girl on tiptoe in a dark room with one fingertip on a wall, a tiny arrow for the touch and a thick arrow for her weight, labelled much smaller.
explanations.context: This card explains the Fingertip test and why light touch steadies you.

explanations.definition: Sometimes a few ear crystals break loose from their pouch and drift into one of the canals. They make the brain think the head is turning, and cause a short spell of spinning.
explanations.description: The ear crystals are meant to stay on their jelly. In some people, mostly adults, a few crystals come loose and roll into a canal. When the person tips their head in a certain way, the crystals slide and push the liquid, just as if the head were turning fast. The person feels the room spin for about a minute. Doctors call this benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which means a harmless spell of spinning that comes with a head position. A doctor can cure it by moving the patient's head through a set of positions that rolls the crystals out of the canal and back into the pouch. One well-known set of moves was described by the American doctor John Epley in 1992. Children rarely get it. If a child has spells of spinning for no reason, a doctor should check.
examples: Rolling over in bed makes the room spin for a few seconds, then it stops.
Looking up quickly to take a coconut from a shelf makes an older person dizzy for a moment.
A doctor guides the head through four positions to move the crystals back.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a canal with a few white crystals rolling along it, and a doctor's hands gently tilting a patient's head.
explanations.context: This card is about what goes wrong when ear crystals leave their pouch.

explanations.concept: Warm and cold gates in the skin
explanations.definition: Warmth and cold are sensed by tiny gates in nerve endings called ion channels. Each kind of gate opens at its own temperature, so different nerve endings report different ranges.
explanations.description: In 1997, the scientist David Julius and his team found the gate that opens for chilli and for heat. It opens when the temperature rises above about 43 degrees Celsius, and also when it meets the chemical in chilli, which is called capsaicin. So a green chilli really does feel hot, because it opens the same gate as hot water would. In 2002, a team led by David McKemy found a gate that opens when it is cool and also opens for menthol, the chemical in mint. Later work found that this gate opens below about 26 degrees Celsius. That is why mint feels cool even though it is not cold. Other gates in the same family open at warm, hot, or very cold temperatures. Julius and Ardem Patapoutian shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for finding the gates for temperature and touch. Your sense of warmth is the combined report of many such gates.
examples: Chilli feels hot because it opens the heat gate.
A peppermint sweet makes your breath feel cool because mint opens the cool gate.
Mustard oil makes the nose sting because it opens another gate, one that warns of harm.
explanations.art: Three nerve endings with gates drawn as small doors: one opening for a hot cup and a chilli, one for an ice cube and a mint leaf, one for a mustard seed.
explanations.context: This card explains how mint and chilli fool the skin, and where warm and cold are sensed.

explanations.definition: The brain adds up warmth from all the places it is felt. The same warmth feels stronger when it touches a larger part of your skin. This is called spatial summation.
explanations.description: Dip a fingertip into bath-warm water, and it feels pleasantly mild. Dip your whole hand into the same water, and it feels warmer. The water has not changed, but many more warm gates have opened, and the brain adds their reports. This is why you test a baby's bath with your elbow or wrist. A larger area of skin gives a clearer message than a fingertip. It is also why a hot water bottle spread over your tummy feels very hot, and why a hot spoon feels less hot when it touches one finger than when your whole hand holds it. This shows that your sense of warmth is not a thermometer. It adds up many reports.
examples: A bath feels hotter to a whole foot than to one toe.
A big sip of hot tea feels hotter than a tiny drop of the same tea.
A warm hand over your cheek feels warmer than one finger on your cheek.
explanations.art: A fingertip and a whole hand dipped in two bowls of the same warm water, with a thermometer showing the same reading and a bigger red bar beside the whole hand.
explanations.context: This card explains the Warm Hand test, where the same water feels different on a finger and on a whole hand.

explanations.concept: Keeping warm and cool: sensing is half of a loop
explanations.definition: Your body keeps its core temperature close to 37 degrees Celsius with a feedback loop. Sensors in the skin and deep in the body measure the temperature, and the brain makes the body warm itself or cool itself.
explanations.description: A part of the brain called the hypothalamus works like a thermostat. It gets reports from temperature sensors in the skin and from the blood passing through it. If your core gets too warm, the brain makes you sweat. Sweat takes heat away as it dries. The brain also widens the blood vessels near the skin, so more heat can leave. If your core gets too cool, the brain narrows those blood vessels, makes your muscles shiver to make heat, and makes the tiny muscles at the base of each hair pull, which gives you goosebumps. Then the sensors check the result again. When you have a fever, the loop is not broken. The brain has raised the level it aims for, so you feel cold and shiver until you reach the higher number. The senses in this loop do more than tell you the temperature. The body uses them to correct it.
examples: After running, you sweat and your face goes red, as the loop sends heat out.
On a cold morning, you shiver and your hairs stand up.
A clay matka keeps water cool because water dries off its walls and takes heat away, much like sweat does.
explanations.art: A circle of four boxes joined by arrows: skin sensors, brain thermostat, sweating or shivering, body temperature, with a child fanning herself in the middle.
explanations.context: This card explains how the body uses its sense of temperature to keep itself near 37 degrees.

explanations.concept: Two kinds of pain, and why rubbing helps
explanations.definition: Pain signals travel along two kinds of nerve fibre. Fast ones carry a sharp signal that shows where you were hurt. Slow ones carry a dull, throbbing signal that lasts longer.
explanations.description: When you stub your toe, you feel two things. First comes a short sharp jab. A moment later comes a dull, spreading throb. The sharp jab travels along thin nerve fibres wrapped in a coat that makes the signal fast. The throb travels along even thinner fibres with no coat, which carry the signal slowly, about as fast as a slow walk. The difference is larger when the hurt is far from the brain, as a toe is. In 1965, Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall suggested that touch signals can turn down pain signals at the spinal cord, like a gate. Scientists have changed many details of this idea since then, but the main point holds: rubbing a bumped elbow really does reduce the pain, because the touch signals compete with the pain signals.
examples: A bumped knee gives a sharp pain first, and a throb after.
Rubbing the spot where you bumped your head makes it hurt less.
A paper cut gives a sharp sting, and then a burning that lingers.
explanations.art: A leg with a stubbed toe and two arrows going up it, a fast sharp one arriving at the brain first and a slow thick one arriving later.
explanations.context: This card explains why a hurt has a sharp part and a throbbing part, and why rubbing helps.

explanations.concept: Pain changes with attention and with the situation
explanations.definition: How much pain you feel depends on more than how much your body is damaged. Attention, fear, hope and the situation all change it.
explanations.description: In 1946, a doctor named Henry Beecher, who had treated wounded soldiers in the Second World War, reported something odd. Many soldiers with serious wounds asked for little or no pain medicine. Civilians with similar wounds from an operation usually asked for much more. Beecher thought that the soldiers felt relief at being alive and away from the battle. Pain is a message about danger, and the brain weighs it against everything else it knows. This idea has been supported by many later tests. People feel less pain when they are distracted, when they trust the person helping them, or when they are not afraid of what the pain means. People feel more when they are worried or when they give the pain all their attention. This does not mean the pain is imaginary. It means the brain builds pain from many clues, not only from the nerve signal.
examples: A child who falls while playing a game often does not notice the scrape until the game is over.
A shot hurts more when you stare at the needle and are scared of it.
Counting backwards in your head can make an ice cube in your hand ache less.
explanations.art: A child running in a game with a scraped knee she has not noticed, and a second picture of the same child crying when she looks at the scrape.
explanations.context: This card explains why the Ice in the Palm test can give different answers when you think about different things.

explanations.concept: Is pain a sense, or something the brain makes?
explanations.description: Nerve endings that react to harm are called nociceptors, and their signals are real and can be measured. But scientists argue about whether pain is the signal or something more. A person can have the signal without pain, as some wounded soldiers do. A person can also have pain without the signal, as when someone feels pain in a limb that is no longer there. This is called a phantom limb. In 2020, the International Association for the Study of Pain gave a new definition: pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience linked to real or possible damage. The debate matters, because it changes how doctors treat long-lasting pain.
examples: A person who has lost a leg can still feel pain in the foot that is no longer there.
A soldier with a serious wound may feel almost no pain at first.
Long-lasting back pain can continue after the back has healed.

perspectives.explanation: Nociceptors are receptors, like those for light or warmth. Pain is what their signals feel like, and it protects the body.

perspectives.who: Pain as an experience the brain builds
perspectives.explanation: The signal from the nociceptors is not yet pain. The brain builds pain from the signal, memory, attention and feelings, so the same signal can feel very different.

explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a nerve ending sending a signal up a nerve to a brain, and the same brain with thought bubbles of fear, memory and attention feeding into the pain.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: whether pain is a sense like sight, or something the brain builds.

explanations.concept: Senses that look inward: your own heartbeat
explanations.definition: Interoception is the sense of what is going on inside you, such as your heartbeat, breathing, hunger, thirst and fullness. People differ a lot in how well they can tell their own heartbeat.
explanations.description: Sensors in the heart, blood vessels, lungs and stomach send signals to the brain all the time. Most of the time you do not notice them. You do notice them when they are strong, such as a pounding heart after running or a growling stomach. In 1981, the researcher Rainer Schandry asked people to count their heartbeats during timed periods, without feeling their pulse, and then compared the count with a real recording. Some people were close, and many were far off. A common mistake is to count too few. Many people do better after exercise, when each beat is stronger. This is not a test of how clever or healthy anyone is. It shows that people differ in how clearly they hear this inner sense, and that it can be practised.
examples: Your heart pounds in your ears after climbing the stairs.
You feel full before you finish your plate when you eat slowly.
You feel thirsty long before your mouth is really dry.
explanations.art: A child sitting quietly with her eyes closed and a hand on her knee, and a glowing heart in her chest with a few small beats drawn around it.
explanations.context: This card explains the Count Your Own Heartbeat activity and the senses that look inward.

explanations.definition: Flies and mosquitoes have two tiny club-shaped stalks behind their wings, called halteres. They swing as the wings beat, and they sense when the body turns.
explanations.description: A fly has only one pair of wings. Where a second pair would be, there are two tiny stalks with a knob at the end. When the fly flies, the halteres beat up and down as fast as the wings, more than a hundred times a second. If the fly's body turns, the swinging clubs are pushed sideways by the turn. Sensors at the base of each club feel the push, and tell the brain how the body is turning. In 1948, the researcher John Pringle published the first detailed study of how halteres work as tiny turning sensors. Flies whose halteres have been removed can still beat their wings, but they cannot fly steadily. They tumble and lose their direction. Our own semicircular canals do a similar job in a very different way. Both feel the body turn, one with swinging clubs, the other with swirling liquid.
examples: A housefly can dodge a swat in the air, because the halteres tell her brain about each turn.
A mosquito turns sharply to follow a smell, using her halteres to keep steady.
A crane fly, the long-legged fly that bumps against lamps, has halteres large enough to see.
explanations.art: A large crane fly from the side with a circle around one tiny club, and an enlarged picture of the club swinging up and down with a small sideways arrow when the body turns.
explanations.context: This card is about a balance sense in flies that works like the canals in your ear.

explanations.concept: Heat pits, and the same gate tuned differently
explanations.definition: Some snakes have heat pits on their faces that sense the warmth given off by a living body. Vampire bats also have a heat sense near their nose. In both, the gate used is one that other animals use for pain or heat.
explanations.description: A pit viper, such as the Malabar pit viper of the Western Ghats, has a pit between each eye and nostril. Pythons have a row of pits along their lips. A thin skin covers each pit, and it warms up when a warm animal is near. The pit works like a very simple pinhole camera, which gives a blurry picture of warm things. In 1937, the researchers Noble and Schmidt showed that rattlesnakes with covered pits did not strike warm objects well. In 2010, a team including Elena Gracheva and David Julius found that the gate in the snake's pit nerves is the same gate that opens for mustard oil in a mouse, but tuned to warmth. In 2011 the same group found that vampire bats have a shorter form of the chilli gate that opens at a lower temperature than ours, so they can find a warm spot on a sleeping animal. Evolution does not always build a new sense. It often takes a gate that already exists and tunes it.
examples: A python finds a warm rat in a dark store room by the heat of her body.
A vampire bat finds the warm skin of a sleeping animal using her nose.
A mosquito flies towards warm skin after she has noticed your breath.
explanations.art: A pit viper's head with a small pit between her eye and her nostril, a warm mouse glowing red in front of her, and a dotted cone showing the field of the pit.
explanations.context: This card is about snakes and bats that sense heat, and how their gates relate to the ones in your own skin.

explanations.concept: Ear stones that keep a diary
explanations.definition: Fish have hard ear stones in their inner ears that help them balance and sense movement. A stone grows a thin layer every day and a thicker layer in good seasons, so it records the fish's life.
explanations.description: Fish have no outer ears, but they have inner ears, and in each one there are hard stones made of calcium carbonate. They rest on sensing hairs. When the fish tilts or speeds up, the stones lag behind, and the hairs bend. This is the same plan as the ear crystals in your own ears, but with bigger and harder stones. The stones also grow, adding thin layers day after day. Scientists cut a thin slice of the stone and count the layers under a microscope. This tells them the age of the fish, and in some cases which waters she lived in. Fisheries scientists use this to learn how long fish like mathi (sardines) live, and whether too many young fish are being caught.
examples: A sardine caught off Kerala has an ear stone that tells her age in days and months.
A rohu in a pond tilts her body and her ear stones press on hairs, just as your crystals do.
A very old fish has an ear stone with many fine layers.
explanations.art: A fish drawn with a magnified circle at the back of her head showing an ear stone with growth rings like a cut tree, and a scientist's hand holding a microscope slide.
explanations.context: This card is about how fish use the same balance idea as you, and how their ear stones record their lives.

agreed.text: Balance comes from the eyes, the inner ears and the sensors in the body together, and the brain gives more weight to the ones that work best.
agreed.evidence: In the 1840s, Moritz Romberg saw that some patients stood well with their eyes open and swayed with them shut. Later, moving floors and moving rooms showed that when one source is made useless, healthy people rely more on the other two.

agreed.text: The canals of the inner ear sense turning, the ear crystals sense tilting and speeding up, and the head-turn reflex uses them to keep the eyes steady.
agreed.evidence: In the 1820s, Pierre Flourens cut the canals of pigeons and saw them tumble. About 1906, Robert Bárány showed that warm or cool water in the ear makes the eyes flick, because it makes the liquid in a canal move. Doctors still use both ideas to test patients.

agreed.text: A fingertip resting on a still object can steady a standing person, even when the touch is far too light to hold them up.
agreed.evidence: In 1994, Jeka and Lackner measured the force of the fingertip and the sway of the body. The force was less than about 1 newton, which is about the weight of a small tomato, and the sway dropped a great deal.

agreed.text: Warmth and cold are sensed by different gates in nerve endings, and each kind of gate opens at its own temperature. The chilli gate also opens for heat, and the mint gate also opens for cool.
agreed.evidence: In 1997 and 2002, scientists put these gates into ordinary cells in a dish. The cells then responded to heat and chilli, or to cool and menthol. The work earned the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

agreed.text: The body keeps its core temperature close to 37 degrees Celsius by sensing it and then acting, through sweating, shivering and changes in blood flow.
agreed.evidence: Thermometers show the core temperature stays within about a degree whether the day is hot or cold. In animal experiments, warming a small part of the brain's thermostat makes the animal pant, and cooling that part makes her shiver.

agreed.text: Pain signals travel at two speeds, so a hurt gives a sharp first pain and a dull second pain.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured the speed of the two kinds of nerve fibre. When a nerve is partly blocked, people lose one of the two pains before the other.

agreed.text: Flies steer with halteres, and some snakes sense warmth with heat pits.
agreed.evidence: In 1948, John Pringle published the first detailed study of how halteres sense turning, and flies without halteres cannot fly steadily. In 1937, Noble and Schmidt covered the pits of rattlesnakes, and the snakes struck warm objects badly.

challenging.claim: The inner ear is the sense of balance, and the eyes and feet only help a little.
challenging.who: Many school books, which show only the ear when they draw balance.
challenging.for: The canals and ear crystals are the only organs built just for balance, and a damaged inner ear causes dizziness.
challenging.against: The eyes and the body sensors do as much of the work. People with damaged inner ears can stand fairly well in the light on a firm floor. Healthy people wobble badly when both eyes and feet are made unreliable.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that balance is only in the ears.

challenging.claim: To stay balanced, a body should hold as still as it can.
challenging.who: Many people, and many children told to 'stand still'.
challenging.for: A body that moves a lot looks as if it is about to fall, so holding still looks safer.
challenging.against: A standing body is always swaying a little and correcting itself. People who freeze up stiffly often balance worse. A steady body moves a little all the time.
challenging.context: This card is about whether standing still means holding perfectly still.

challenging.claim: A walking stick is only a support, and needing one means you are weak.
challenging.who: Many people who feel unsteady but do not want a stick, and some of their families.
challenging.for: A stick can take weight off a sore knee or hip.
challenging.against: A stick that is touched lightly works as a sensor, as a fingertip on a wall does. It adds a fourth source of balance information. Using one is a way of using the body's senses well.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a walking stick is a prop or a sense organ.

challenging.claim: Hot and cold are the two ends of one feeling, sensed by the same nerve endings.
challenging.who: A common idea, because warm and cold seem like opposites.
challenging.for: Warming a cold hand feels like the reverse of cooling a hot hand, as if both were one feeling going in two directions.
challenging.against: The skin has separate gates for cold and for warmth, in different places. Chilli opens a heat gate and mint opens a cool gate, and neither changes the temperature.
challenging.context: This card is about whether warm and cold are one sense.

challenging.claim: A fever means the body has lost control of its temperature.
challenging.who: Many worried people, when a child feels very hot.
challenging.for: The child is hot and uncomfortable, and the temperature is not normal.
challenging.against: In a fever, the brain's thermostat is set higher on purpose, so the body shivers to reach the higher number. The control loop works. A very high fever or a long one still needs a doctor.
challenging.context: This card is about what is really happening in the body during a fever.

challenging.claim: How much pain you feel always matches how much damage was done.
challenging.who: Many people, because pain feels like a direct reading of the damage.
challenging.for: Bigger injuries usually hurt more than small ones.
challenging.against: Wounded soldiers have reported little pain, while small cuts hurt a great deal. A phantom limb hurts although the limb is gone. The brain weighs pain against fear, attention and what the hurt means.
challenging.context: This card is about whether pain measures the damage to the body.

big_questions.q: In the Balance Team test, you wobbled the most on a blanket with your eyes shut. If no single part of you holds you upright, where does the feeling of being upright come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about three sources of information and the brain that mixes them.

big_questions.q: In A Fingertip Lighter than a Tomato, a touch lighter than a tomato steadied your whole body, though it held none of your weight. Can something that carries no weight still help a great deal?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between a push and a message.

big_questions.q: The train beside yours starts to move. Your eyes say your train is moving, and your ears say it is still. Which one is right, and how could you check?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each sense measures, and what a third check might be.

big_questions.q: A python senses heat, a fly feels turning with two tiny clubs, and a bee sees ultraviolet light. Do they live in the same world as you, seen with different senses, or in different worlds?
big_questions.hint: Think of a red fruit. To you it looks red. To a bee it looks black and ultraviolet.

big_questions.q: A green chilli opens the same gate in your tongue as hot water does. Is the chilli hot?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the word hot refers to: the chilli, the gate, or the feeling.

big_questions.q: The same bump can be a big pain on one day and a small pain on another. Which of the two is the real pain?
big_questions.hint: Think about how attention, fear and trust change the feeling.

big_questions.q: Dancers and gymnasts practise balance for years. Do they gain a new sense, or do they learn to use the same senses better?
big_questions.hint: Think about the three sources of information and how the brain might weigh them.

big_questions.q: Your body keeps its heat steady by sensing and then acting. What else in a body, a family or a village is kept steady by sensing and acting?
big_questions.hint: Think about thirst, a thermostat, a pot on the stove, or a shopkeeper who watches the stock.

big_questions.q: Obaid Siddiqi, a scientist from Uttar Pradesh who started India's National Centre for Biological Sciences, studied how fruit flies sense their world. Why might a fly teach us something about a child?
big_questions.hint: Think about gates and genes that animals have in common.

story.title: The Stick Nobody Leaned On
story.note: The story is made up, and the people in it are not real. The science is true. In 1994, John Jeka and James Lackner reported that a fingertip resting on a still rail, with less than about 1 newton of force, steadies a standing person. Using a walking stick lightly, as a sensor, has been studied in older people. The kitchen scale in the story is a classroom idea, not part of the 1994 study.
text: Meenakshi was nine, and every Pongal holiday she took the night bus to Madurai to stay with her Paati. Paati's house was tall and narrow and old, with a courtyard in the middle open to the sky. The rooms stood around it like children sitting round a mat.

Meenakshi's mother said that Paati used to walk down to the river Vaigai every morning, with a bag of flowers for the temple. This year she did not go. She said her knees were tired. But Meenakshi saw how Paati stood at the front door each morning, looking at the street, and then turned back in.
Behind the front door a new walking stick leaned against the wall. Meenakshi's uncle had brought it from Chennai. It was shiny and brown, with a rubber foot. Nobody ever touched it.
"That thing is for old people," said Paati, when Meenakshi asked about it. "I am not old. I am only slow."
On the third evening, the power went out. The fan stopped. The whole street went dark at once, and somewhere a dog barked at nothing.
"Meenu, my spectacles are on the bed," Paati said. "I will get them." She stood up and walked to the kitchen door, where the passage to the bedroom began. Then she stopped.

The passage ran along the courtyard. It was only six steps long, and Meenakshi had run along it a hundred times. But Paati stood at the end with one hand on the doorframe, and did not move. In the light of Meenakshi's phone torch, her face looked small.
"I can't," Paati said. "The floor has gone away."
"It's right there, Paati. I'm lighting it."

"My eyes can see it," said Paati. "My feet do not believe it. When there is light, my feet listen to my eyes. In the dark, they have nobody to listen to. And they have grown quiet, these old feet. They used to tell me everything."

Meenakshi thought hard. Something was tugging at her memory. Last month, in school, Sridevi Miss had made them stand in a line, one foot in front of the other, heel to toe, with their eyes shut. Everyone had swayed like banana plants in the wind. Then Sridevi Miss had said, "Now touch the wall with one finger. Do not push. Only touch."

And the swaying had stopped. It felt so strange. Her finger had hardly rested on the wall, and yet she stood like a pillar. Sridevi Miss had put a kitchen scale on a shelf and asked a girl to touch it the same way. The numbers hardly moved. "That is lighter than a tomato," she had said. "It cannot hold you up. So what is it doing?"
Nobody in the class had known. Meenakshi did not know either. But she knew that it worked.
"Paati," she said, "put one finger on the wall. Do not lean. Touch it softly, as if you are checking that a baby is asleep."
"What nonsense is this?" said Paati. But she lifted her hand from the doorframe, and laid one fingertip on the cool, rough wall.

She took a step. Then another. Her finger slid along the wall like a boat on a still river. Her shoulders came down. Her steps grew longer. By the end of the passage, she was nearly walking the way she used to.
She found her spectacles. She came back the same way, finger on the wall. At the kitchen door she stopped, and laughed out loud, a laugh Meenakshi had not heard all year.
"It is not holding me up," Paati said. "I can feel that it is not. I could pull my finger away this minute. But my feet are listening again."
"Your finger tells them where you are," said Meenakshi. "The wall stays still, so it is easy to tell." She was surprised to hear herself say it.

The next morning, Paati went to the front door and took the shiny stick from behind it. She looked at it as she might look at a cousin she had not spoken to for years. "I will not lean on you," she told it. "I will only touch the ground with you. You can be my finger."

Then she walked all the way to the river, with Meenakshi beside her. The stick went tik, tik, tik on the road, as light as a whisper. Paati held it so softly that a passing girl thought she was carrying it for fun. Each time the rubber foot touched the road, her feet knew a little more about where they were.
At the Vaigai, an old man on the steps looked at the stick and then at Paati. "Is that for the knees?" he asked. "No," said Paati. "It is for feet that have gone quiet."
story.epiphany: For the parent: a fingertip resting on something still gives the brain a fourth source of balance information, because a still wall tells the body exactly how it is moving. In 1994, John Jeka and James Lackner found that the touch steadies people even when its force is under about 1 newton, far too little to hold anyone up. A walking stick that is touched lightly works the same way. It is a sensor, not a prop.
ask: Why can one fingertip on a still wall steady a person who is not leaning on it?
In the dark passage, which two of Paati's three balance sources were weak or missing, and which one was left?
What is the difference between a stick you lean on and a stick you only touch?
How could a family make the night path to the toilet easier for a grandparent who feels unsteady?
art: A tall narrow old house in Madurai with an open courtyard, a girl and her grandmother on the veranda at dusk, and a shiny brown stick leaning behind the front door.
A dark passage beside the courtyard lit only by a phone torch, with an older woman standing frozen at the kitchen door with one hand on the frame.
A classroom in which children stand heel to toe with eyes shut, one child touching the wall with a fingertip and a kitchen scale on a shelf nearby.
An older woman walking along a lime-washed wall with one fingertip on it, and a girl holding the torch behind her.
The same grandmother walking beside the river steps in the morning, holding a stick so lightly that only its rubber foot touches the road.

games.title: Which Sense Was Fooled?
games.context: This is a card game about the balance team. Each card describes a moment, and you decide which of your three balance sources is fooled, missing or unsure.

printables.title: 20 moment cards: the moment on the front, the answer and reason on the back

items.f: You sit in a train at a station. The train beside yours slowly starts to move.
items.b: EYES are fooled. They show movement, but your ears and feet say you are still. For a moment you feel your own train sliding.

items.f: You stand in a pitch-dark room on a hard floor.
items.b: EYES give no information. Your ears and feet still work, so you can stand, but you sway more.

items.f: You stand on a thick folded mattress with your eyes open.
items.b: FEET AND MUSCLES are less sure on soft ground. Your eyes and ears make up for them.

items.f: You stand on a thick folded mattress with your eyes shut.
items.b: EYES give nothing and FEET AND MUSCLES are unsure. Only the ears are reliable, so this is the hardest case.

items.f: You spin round ten times and then stop.
items.b: INNER EARS are fooled. The liquid in the canals keeps swirling, so they say you are still turning.

items.f: You read a comic in a bus on a winding road.
items.b: EYES say you are still, while INNER EARS feel every turn. The mismatch can make you feel sick.

items.f: You watch a film of a roller coaster, and lean with the curves, though your seat is still.
items.b: EYES are fooled. The picture says you are moving, but your ears and seat say you are still.

items.f: A lift moves up at a steady speed with the doors closed.
items.b: NOBODY is fooled. The inner ears feel only the start and the stop, not the steady part, so you cannot tell you are moving.

items.f: Your foot has fallen asleep after you sat cross-legged.
items.b: FEET AND MUSCLES are not sending clear messages. Your eyes and ears have to help you stand.

items.f: You try on a friend's very strong glasses, and the floor seems to curve.
items.b: EYES are giving a bent picture. Your ears and feet say the floor is flat, so you feel unsteady until your brain adjusts.

items.f: You walk on soft sand at the beach with your eyes open.
items.b: FEET AND MUSCLES are less sure on soft sand. Your eyes and ears help.

items.f: You stand on a boat deck looking at the horizon.
items.b: NOBODY is fooled. Your eyes see the same rocking that your ears feel, so the messages agree and the sickness eases.

items.f: An astronaut floats inside a space station.
items.b: INNER EARS give odd messages. In free fall the ear crystals do not press down on their jelly, so they cannot say which way is down.

items.f: A toddler stands in a room whose walls slide forward while the floor stays still.
items.b: EYES are fooled. They say the toddler is moving forward, so she leans back, though she is not moving.

items.f: You are in a bus that brakes hard, and you lean forward without thinking.
items.b: NOBODY is fooled. Your ears and body sensors feel the slowing, and your brain corrects at once.

items.f: You tilt your head to one side and keep reading a book without trouble.
items.b: NOBODY is fooled. The head-turn reflex uses your inner ears to keep your eyes steady on the page.

items.f: A fog hides the horizon from a ship, and you feel unsteady.
items.b: EYES have little to see, so their information is weak. Your inner ears feel the rolling of the ship, and the messages do not match.

items.f: You rock in a hammock with your eyes open, and you feel fine.
items.b: NOBODY is fooled. The messages from your eyes, ears and body all agree.

items.f: You stand on one foot to put on a sock, and then you shut your eyes by mistake.
items.b: EYES are lost. Your ears and feet must take over, and you wobble more.

items.f: You step off a merry-go-round that has been spinning for a while.
items.b: INNER EARS are fooled for a few seconds, because the liquid keeps swirling. Your eyes and the ground say you are still.

printables.title: 4 answer tokens (print this page once for each player)

rules: Each player has the four answer tokens. Stack the 20 moment cards with the moment side up.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the moment aloud, and keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts down one token face down. It shows which source is fooled, missing or unsure, or that nobody is.
The reader reads the back aloud. Everyone turns their token up. Each right token scores 1 point.
Some cards name two sources. If your token is one of them, you score.
Each player who scored gives one sentence that says what the brain does with the messages. A good reason scores 1 extra point.
The reader job passes round after each card. When the cards run out, the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.
If you play alone, read a moment, put down a token, and check the back. Count your score out of 20.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and tokens. Stack the cards with the moment side up. Give each player four tokens.
flow.parent: A grown-up helps younger children with the scissors. The moments on the cards are only imagined, so nobody has to try them for real. Do not spin or stand on a mattress to check a card.
flow.say: Your balance has three helpers. They are your eyes, your inner ears, and your feet and muscles. For each moment, which helper is fooled, missing or unsure?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Each player takes four tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Sense Was Fooled?, a card game about the three sources of balance.

flow.do: Play the first five cards. After each one, ask for a reason before the next card.
flow.say: Read the moment. Everyone chooses a token and puts it face down. Now turn it up. What does the brain do with the messages?
flow.kid: Read a moment. Pick a token and put it face down. Turn it up, then check the back of the card.

ask.q: Why is the mattress with eyes shut harder than the mattress with eyes open?
good: With eyes open the eyes help the unsure feet.
With eyes shut only the ears are left.
Two helpers are missing, so there is less to go on.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first five cards and learn how the scoring works.

flow.do: Play the next ten cards. Keep a tally of the points. Notice which token is chosen most often.
flow.say: Keep going. Which helper is fooled most often in these cards? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Play ten more cards. Count the points.
flow.parent: Look at which token was chosen most. Eyes are named in many cards, because a moving picture can fool them easily. Feet are often unsure rather than fooled. Inner ears are fooled by spinning and by floating in space.
flow.context: In this step, you play the middle cards of the game and look for a pattern.

flow.do: Play the last five cards. Add up the scores. Ask the closing question.
flow.say: Add up your points. When two helpers disagree, which one does your brain believe? Does it always believe the same one?
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Add up your points.

ask.q: When two helpers disagree, which one does the brain believe?
good: The one that is usually more reliable.
Sometimes the eyes, as with the train.
It changes, depending on the moment.

flow.context: In this step, you finish the cards and think about which helper the brain trusts.

flow.do: Ask the check question. Discuss the answer.
flow.say: Let us check one more moment before we finish.
flow.kid: Answer the check question.

check.q: A child reads a book in a moving car and feels sick. Which pair of helpers disagree?
options: Her eyes and her inner ears
Her feet and her nose
Her eyes and her ears working together
check.why: Her eyes see a book that is still, while her inner ears feel the car turning and bumping. When these two do not match, the brain gets confused and she may feel sick. Looking out at the horizon can make them agree again.

flow.context: In this step, you check one more moment with a question.

setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Stack the cards.

setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a moment. Everyone else chooses a token.

setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens up and check the back of the card.

games.title: Wobble Relay: stations that take a helper away
games.context: This is a movement game about the balance team. At each station, one of your three balance helpers is taken away, and you see how long you can stay steady.

printables.title: 6 station cards: the pose on the front, which helper is taken away on the back

items.f: STATION 1: Stand on one foot with your arms folded across your chest, eyes open, on the bare floor.
items.b: Nothing is taken away. This is your starting score.

items.f: STATION 2: Stand on one foot with your arms folded, eyes shut, on the bare floor.
items.b: Your eyes are taken away. Your ears and feet must do the job.

items.f: STATION 3: Stand on one foot with your arms folded, eyes open, on a folded blanket.
items.b: Your feet are made unsure by the soft surface. Your eyes and ears help.

items.f: STATION 4: Stand on one foot with your eyes shut, and rest one fingertip lightly on a wall.
items.b: Your eyes are taken away as at station 2, but a fourth helper is added: light touch on a still wall.

items.f: STATION 5: Stand on one foot with your arms folded, eyes open, and look up at the ceiling.
items.b: Looking up makes the picture from your eyes less useful, and changes the signals from your neck and ears.

items.f: STATION 6: Stand heel to toe in a line, eyes open, with your arms folded.
items.b: Your base is made narrow. All three helpers work hard.

printables.title: Score sheet for the relay
items: Total points: 1 point for each full 5 seconds, at most 4 per station

rules: Set out six stations in a clear space on a mat or carpet, away from stairs and furniture. Place the station cards by each one.
A grown-up or a friend stays beside the player as a spotter at every station, ready to catch.
At each station the player takes the pose and the timer starts. The timer stops when the player's raised foot touches the floor, when the player moves a foot, or at 20 seconds.
Score 1 point for each full 5 seconds, so a station is worth 0 to 4 points. The most you can win in the relay is 24 points.
Each player visits all six stations. Rest about 15 seconds between stations, and longer if you feel wobbly.
After the relay, each player says which station was hardest and which helper was taken away there.
If you play alone, ask someone to be your timer and spotter, and try to beat your own total on another day.
Anyone who feels dizzy, or has a problem with their ears, watches or times for the others.

flow.do: Set out the six stations. Fold a blanket three times and flatten it for station 3. One spotter walks beside the player from station to station.
flow.say: We will visit six stations. At each one, a helper for your balance is taken away. Which station do you think will be hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Set out six stations. Guess which will be the hardest.

ask.q: Which station do you think will be hardest, and why?
good: The one with my eyes shut, because I cannot see.
The one on the blanket, because the floor is soft.
The one where I look up, because my head is tipped back.

flow.parent: Write down the guess before starting. Stations 2 and 5 are often hard, and station 4 often feels easier than station 2. Results differ with every child.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wobble Relay. You set up six stations and guess which will be hardest.

flow.do: Each player visits stations 1 to 6 in order. A helper times each one with a phone and stops at 20 seconds. Write down the seconds.
flow.say: Take the pose. I will start the timer. Stop when your foot touches down. Rest. Then we go to the next station.
flow.kid: Take the pose at each station. Hold it as long as you can.
flow.parent: Stand close at every station and be ready to catch. Do not let anyone near stairs or furniture. If a child feels dizzy, stop and sit down at once. One player takes about 4 minutes if the rests are short (about 15 seconds). With two to four children, one plays while a second spots, a third times and a fourth writes the seconds, and then you rotate. With one child, the parent spots and times. Station 5, looking up, is the one most likely to make a child fall, so keep the spotter's hands ready.
flow.context: In this step, you play the relay and write down the seconds for each station.

flow.do: Add up the points. Ask which station was hardest, and which helper was taken away there.
flow.say: Add up your points. Which station had the lowest score? Which helper was missing there? What happened at station 4?
flow.kid: Add your points. Which station was hardest?

check.q: At station 4 you stand on one foot with your eyes shut and touch a wall with one finger. Why is this often easier than station 2?
options: The fingertip gives the brain a fourth source of information
The wall holds your weight
Your eyes work even when they are shut
check.why: A light fingertip on a still wall tells the brain exactly how your body is moving. It is too light to hold your weight, but the information helps. This is not the wall holding you up. It is the wall acting as a sense.

flow.context: In this step, you add up the scores and compare the stations.

setup.caption: 2. Take the pose. A grown-up times you and stands close.

setup.art: A score sheet with six rows of seconds and a column of points.
setup.caption: 3. Write the seconds and add up the points.

experiments.title: The Balance Team: what happens when a helper is taken away?
experiments.question: How long can you stand on one foot with your eyes open or shut, on the bare floor or on a folded blanket? Which helper matters most?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In which of the four tests will you wobble the most, and in which the least? Will losing two helpers at once be twice as bad? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every try uses the same pose: the same foot on the floor, the other foot lifted a hand's width, and arms folded. The room, the timer and the spotter stay the same. You rest for one minute between tries. You do the four tests in one order first, and in the opposite order second, so tiredness and practice affect every test equally. Only two things change: whether your eyes are open, and whether the floor is bare or soft.
results_table: Which helpers were still working well?

materials.item: a clear space on a carpet or a mat, about 2 metres wide, away from stairs, tables and sharp corners
a thick blanket or quilt, folded until it is about 5 centimetres thick, or two folded towels
a phone with a stopwatch
a grown-up who stands right beside the child as a spotter for every try
a sheet of paper and a pencil for the results table
a clean scarf to cover the eyes, if the child prefers not to just shut them

experiments.safety: A grown-up stands right beside your child for every try, ready to catch. Do the test on a carpet or mat, away from stairs, tables and sharp corners. Lay the blanket so that it cannot slide. Stop at once if your child feels dizzy or unwell. A child with an ear infection or a balance problem should only time and watch.

schedule.what: Guess, set up, do the four tests twice, draw the bars and explain the result.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Take the best of the two tries for each test. Draw four bars, one for each test, and write under each bar which helpers were still working well.

flow.do: Show your child the four tests. Ask for a guess and a reason for each question. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will stand on one foot four ways. Eyes open or shut, and bare floor or blanket. Which test will be hardest? Which easiest? Why?
flow.kid: You will stand on one foot four ways. Which will be hardest? Which easiest? Why?

ask.q: Which test do you think will be hardest, and why do you think so?
good: Eyes shut on the blanket, because I lose two helpers.
Eyes shut, because I cannot see where I am.
The blanket, because the floor is soft and wobbly.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write down what your child says about two helpers being lost at once. With two to four children, each child has their own table. While one child stands, a second is the spotter, a third times, and a fourth writes the seconds. Then rotate. Compare every child's bars, since the pattern matters more than the seconds.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Balance Team test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Clear the space. Fold the blanket to about 5 centimetres thick and lay it flat on the carpet. Show your child the pose and how a try ends.
flow.say: Fold your arms. Lift one foot a hand's width. A try ends when the foot touches down, you hop, or you hold on to me. The longest a try can last is 30 seconds.
flow.kid: Fold your arms. Lift one foot. The try ends when your foot touches down.
flow.parent: Stand close, with one hand ready near your child's shoulder but not touching. Use the same foot for every try. Practise once with eyes open so the pose is familiar. If your child peeks, cover their eyes with a clean scarf.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the space and learn the pose. Every test uses the same pose.

flow.do: Round 1. Test A: eyes open, bare floor. Test B: eyes shut, bare floor. Test C: eyes open, blanket. Test D: eyes shut, blanket. Time each try. Rest one minute between tries.
flow.say: Round one. Test A: eyes open on the bare floor. Go. Now rest. Test B: eyes shut on the bare floor. Go. Rest. Then test C, eyes open on the blanket, and test D, eyes shut on the blanket.
flow.kid: Do tests A, B, C and D in that order. Rest between tries.
flow.parent: Stop the watch the instant the raised foot touches down, or at 30 seconds. Write the seconds in the table. If your child holds 30 seconds in every test, make the pose harder by standing heel to toe in a line with arms folded, and start again.
flow.context: In this step, you do the first round of four tests and write down the seconds.

flow.do: Round 2. Do the tests in the opposite order: D, C, B, A. Rest one minute between tries. Write the seconds. Pick the best of the two tries for each test.
flow.say: Now round two, backwards. D, then C, then B, then A. We go backwards so that tiredness affects every test equally.
flow.kid: Do the tests backwards. D, C, B, A. Rest between tries.
flow.parent: Watch for the child leaning hard to one side or hopping. Note it in the table. If your child tires or feels dizzy, stop and carry on later.
flow.context: In this step, you repeat the four tests in the opposite order, so the test is fair.

flow.do: Draw a bar for the best time in each test. Look for the longest and shortest bars. Compare with the guess.
flow.say: Look at your bars. Which test gave the longest time? Which the shortest? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each test. Which bar is longest? Which is shortest?
flow.parent: A common pattern is the longest time for eyes open on the floor and the shortest for eyes shut on the blanket. Eyes shut on the floor and eyes open on the blanket often fall between. If your results differ, write them down as they are. A pattern that surprises you is worth explaining.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the results and compare them with your guess.

flow.do: Ask your child what they think happened, what they saw that shows it, and why it happened. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: What do you think was happening? What did you see? Why did eyes shut on the blanket give the shortest time?
flow.kid: Say what you think happened. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

check.q: Why is standing with eyes shut on a soft blanket the hardest?
options: Two of the three helpers are weak, so only the ears are left
The blanket makes you heavier
Your ears stop working when your eyes are shut
check.why: With your eyes shut there is no information from sight. The soft blanket makes the signals from your feet less clear. That leaves your inner ears as the only clear helper, so you wobble most. The ears still work with eyes shut, and the blanket does not change your weight.

flow.context: In this step, you explain the result and check your reasoning.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you stand on one foot four ways, and find out which of your three balance helpers you rely on most.

experiments.title: Shake the Head or Shake the Page?
experiments.question: Can you read as well when your head shakes as when the page shakes by the same amount? What is different about the two?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many words can you read in 10 seconds when your head shakes, and how many when the page shakes? Which will be harder? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You use lines of print of the same size and length, drawn out of a bowl so that no line is always used for the same test. You shake the head or the page side to side at the same beat, about two shakes every second, by about the same distance. The page is held the same distance from your eyes every time. You read for 10 seconds each time. The only thing that changes is what moves: your head or the page.
results_table: Words read right in round 1 (out of 8)
Words read right in round 2 (out of 8)

materials.item: a newspaper or a book with large print, letters about 1 centimetre tall
six lines of print with eight words each, marked with a pencil or sticky notes and numbered 1 to 6
six small slips of paper numbered 1 to 6, folded, in a bowl
a chair for the child to sit on
a phone with a stopwatch, and a pencil and paper for the table
a grown-up to hold the page and count the beat

experiments.safety: Shake your head in small, quick turns, as if saying no, and not hard. Stop at once if your neck hurts or you feel dizzy. Do not spin or shake anyone's head for them. A child with a neck problem or a balance problem should only hold the page and count.

schedule.what: Guess, then read lines three ways, twice each: with head and page still, with your head shaking, and with the page shaking.

experiments.record: Write the words read right for each line. Add the two rounds for each test. Draw three bars, one for each test.

flow.do: Show your child the page and the three tests. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will read in three ways. Head still and page still. Head shaking and page still. Head still and page shaking. Which will be hardest? Why?
flow.kid: You will read three ways. Which will be hardest? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think shaking the page might be harder than shaking your head?
good: It is the same movement, so it should be the same.
The page moves faster than my head.
My eyes can keep up with my head but not with the page.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children guess that both will be equally hard, and that is a fine guess to test. One child alone works with a parent holding the page. With two to four children, one reads, one shakes the page, one counts the beat and one counts the words right. Then rotate. Each reader does all three tests, so each has their own table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Shake the Head or Shake the Page test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Mark six lines of eight words each on the page. Number them. Put six numbered slips in a bowl. Sit your child on a chair. Hold the page level with the eyes, about 40 centimetres away.
flow.say: Here are six lines with eight words each. We draw a slip to pick the line, so the choice is fair. Sit up straight. The page is at your eye level.
flow.kid: Sit on a chair. The page is held at your eye level.
flow.parent: Check that the print is big enough to read easily when still. Letters about 1 centimetre tall work well. Practise the beat: say 'one and two and', two side-to-side shakes in each second.
flow.context: In this step, you prepare six lines of print and set your child on a chair.

flow.do: Test 1: head and page still. Draw a slip, read that line aloud for 10 seconds, and count the words read right. Do it twice. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Head still, page still. Draw a slip. Read the line aloud as well as you can in 10 seconds. Ready, go.
flow.kid: Keep still. Read your line aloud for 10 seconds.
flow.parent: Count a word only if it is read correctly. The first test shows your child's best reading, so you can compare the other two with it. Do not return slips to the bowl until all six are used.
flow.context: In this step, you read with the head and page still, as a starting point.

flow.do: Test 2: shake the head. Test 3: shake the page. For test 2, you hold the page still. Your child shakes their head from side to side, as if saying no, to the beat. For test 3, your child keeps their head still. You shake the page about 5 centimetres each way, to the same beat. Read for 10 seconds, twice each.
flow.say: Test two. Shake your head as if saying no, no, no, to my beat, while you read. Test three. Keep your head still. I will shake the page to the same beat.
flow.kid: Shake your head to the beat and read. Then keep still while the page shakes.
flow.parent: Keep both beats the same. Write what the print looked like each time, such as clear, smeared or jumping. Stop if your child feels dizzy. If both tests are easy, shake faster. If both are impossible, shake more slowly. The head-shake test is easier than it sounds only if the shakes are small and quick. The exact numbers vary a lot, and the page shake is almost always the harder one.
flow.context: In this step, you read with the head shaking and then with the page shaking, to the same beat.

flow.do: Add the two rounds for each test. Draw three bars. Compare the head shake with the page shake. Ask your child what they think happened, what they saw that shows it, and why it happened. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Which was harder, the head or the page? Both moved the same amount at the same beat. What do you think your eyes were doing differently?
flow.kid: Add up your words. Which was harder, head or page? Why?
flow.parent: A common result is that a shaking head makes reading only a little harder, and a shaking page makes it much harder. If so, the head-turn reflex is working: the inner ears tell the eyes to move opposite to the head within a hundredth of a second. Following a moving page on purpose is slower. If your results are the same for both, the shakes may have been too gentle. Shake faster and try again.

check.q: Why can you read while your head shakes, but not when the page shakes at the same beat?
options: Your inner ears move your eyes the opposite way almost at once when your head moves
Your eyes can follow anything that moves quickly
A shaking head makes the print bigger
check.why: When your head turns, the canals in your inner ear start the head-turn reflex, which swings your eyes the other way within about a hundredth of a second. When the page shakes, nothing tells your eyes in advance. They must follow on purpose, which is much slower, and the print smears. Eyes cannot follow a quick movement on their own, and a shaking head does not make the print bigger.

flow.context: In this step, you add up the words, compare the head and page, and explain what you found.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you read while your head shakes, and then while the page shakes, to find out what your inner ears do for your eyes.
