experiments.title: Ice in the Palm: does thinking about something else change the ache?
experiments.question: Does an ice cube in your palm ache less when you count backwards than when you only watch it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After 20 seconds, will the ache be less, the same or more when you count backwards? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every try uses an ice cube of the same size, wrapped in the same kind of thin cloth, held in the same palm for exactly 20 seconds. You rest for three minutes between tries, until the hand is warm and its colour is back. You do the two kinds of try in the order watch, count, count, watch, so that a second try is not always the same kind. The only thing that changes is what your mind does.
results_table: What the mind did (watch or count)

materials.item: 4 ice cubes of the same size, from one tray, kept in the freezer and taken out one at a time just before each try, since in hot weather they melt in minutes
4 thin cotton cloths or handkerchiefs, each big enough to wrap one ice cube
a small bowl to drop the ice into, and a towel to dry the hand
a phone with a stopwatch
a sheet of paper with a line drawn from 0 to 10 and a pencil
a grown-up to watch the whole time

experiments.safety: Ice can hurt the skin if it is held too long. Always wrap the cube in a thin cloth, and drop it after exactly 20 seconds. Your child may drop it sooner, at any moment, and nobody should tell them to hold on. Do not do this test if your child's hands turn white or blue in the cold, or if there is a skin problem on the hand. The palm may look pink for a few minutes. Wait until it is warm before the next try.

schedule.what: Guess, practise the counting, then four 20-second tries with three-minute rests.

experiments.record: After each try, write the ache from 0 to 10. 0 means no ache, and 10 means you wanted to drop the cube at once. Write the colour of the palm. Then compare the two watch tries with the two count tries.

flow.do: Show your child the ice, the cloth and the scale from 0 to 10. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write them down.
flow.say: We will hold an ice cube for 20 seconds. Sometimes you will only watch it. Sometimes you will count backwards. Will the ache change? Why?
flow.kid: You will hold an ice cube for 20 seconds. Will counting change the ache? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think counting might change how much the ice aches?
good: My mind is busy, so I notice the ache less.
Nothing will change, because the ice is the same.
Counting would make it worse, because I have to concentrate.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Remind your child that the cube can be dropped at any moment, and that nothing bad will happen if they drop it. With two to four children, each child has their own cubes and their own scale from 0 to 10. One child holds, a second times, and a third is the grown-up's helper. Each child gives the rating quietly or on paper, so others do not hear the number first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ice in the Palm test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Practise the counting without ice. Count backwards from 50 in twos, aloud: 50, 48, 46. Show how to wrap a cube in a thin cloth and hold it in the open palm.
flow.say: First, count backwards from fifty in twos, with no ice. Fifty, forty-eight, forty-six. Say it aloud. This must be easy before we add the ice.
flow.kid: Count backwards from 50 in twos. Say it out loud.
flow.parent: If counting by twos is too hard, use counting backwards from 20 in ones, or saying the days of the week backwards. The task should keep the mind busy but not be frightening.
flow.context: In this step, you practise the counting task before any ice is used.

flow.do: Try 1 (watch): your child holds a wrapped cube in the open palm and watches the cube and the stopwatch for 20 seconds. Then drop the cube in the bowl. Ask for the ache from 0 to 10. Rest three minutes. Try 2 (count): the same, but counting backwards aloud.
flow.say: Try one. Hold the ice. Only watch it and think about the cold. Ready, go. Drop it. How much did it ache, from zero to ten? Rest now.
flow.kid: Hold the ice and only watch it. Drop it at 20 seconds. Say the ache from 0 to 10.
flow.parent: Stop the watch at exactly 20 seconds and tell your child to drop the cube. Write the number your child gives, and look at the palm. A pink palm is normal. Dry the hand with the towel, and let it warm fully before the next try.
flow.context: In this step, you do the first two tries: one watching and one counting.

flow.do: Try 3 (count) and Try 4 (watch), with three minutes of rest between. Write the ache and the colour of the palm each time.
flow.say: Try three, counting backwards from fifty in twos. Try four, only watching again. We swap the order so that the second try is not always the same kind.
flow.kid: Do a counting try, then a watching try. Rest between them.
flow.parent: If your child keeps losing count, note it. Busy minds do not always count well. Do not push for a specific answer. A rating that does not change is a result too.
flow.context: In this step, you do the last two tries, in the opposite order.

flow.do: Add the two watch ratings and the two count ratings. Compare them. Ask your child what they think happened, what they saw that shows it, and why it happened. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Add the two watch tries. Add the two count tries. Which is bigger? What does that tell you about the ache, and about where it comes from?
flow.kid: Add the watch tries. Add the count tries. Which is bigger?
flow.parent: If the watch tries hardly ache at all (below 2), use a thinner cloth next time, but never hold longer than 20 seconds. Many children give a lower number when they count, typically by one to three points, but some give the same and a few give higher. The ache is real in every case. The brain turns the ache up or down depending on how much attention it has for it. Pain is not an exact measure of the cold or the damage.

check.q: If counting backwards lowered the ache from the ice, what would that show?
options: Attention changes how strong a pain feels
The ice was not really cold
Counting makes the ice melt faster
check.why: The cold was the same in both tries, but the felt ache was lower when the mind was busy. This suggests that the brain builds pain from the signal and from attention. The ice was just as cold, and counting does not melt ice. Your result may differ, and that is worth writing down.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the two kinds of try and explain what you found.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you hold an ice cube for 20 seconds while watching or while counting backwards, and find out whether attention changes the ache.

activities.title: Under the Spinning Umbrella: does the world turn you?
activities.safety: A grown-up holds the umbrella and keeps the metal tips away from your child's face and eyes. Turn it slowly. Use a steady chair, away from stairs and sharp corners. Stop at once if your child feels dizzy or sick.

materials.item: a large umbrella with a pattern or stripes on the inside, opened fully
a steady chair without wheels, or a mat on the floor
a grown-up to turn the umbrella and stay beside the child
sticky paper dots or a marker, if the umbrella is plain, to make a pattern on the inside

schedule.what: Guess, sit under the umbrella while it turns slowly, say what you feel, and swap.

activities.record: Write what each person felt: nothing, a little turning, or a lot. Write whether the feeling was of the umbrella turning, or of the child turning.
activities.context: In this activity, you sit under a turning umbrella and find out whether what you see can make you feel that you are moving.

setup.art: A plain black umbrella opened upside down on a table with white paper dots being stuck on its inside.
setup.caption: 1. If the umbrella is plain, stick dots or stripes on the inside.

setup.art: A girl sitting on a steady chair holding the seat with both hands, an umbrella held low over her head by a grown-up.
setup.caption: 2. Sit on a steady chair. The umbrella covers your view above.

setup.art: The grown-up slowly turning the umbrella handle, with a curved arrow around the umbrella, and the girl looking up.
setup.caption: 3. The grown-up turns the umbrella slowly. Look up at the pattern.

flow.do: Show your child the umbrella. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: I will turn this umbrella slowly over your head while you sit still. Will you feel anything? Will you feel the umbrella turning, or yourself turning?
flow.kid: An umbrella will turn above you. Will you feel anything? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think you might feel something, when you are not moving?
good: My eyes will see the pattern turning.
My brain might think I am the one turning.
I will not feel anything, because I am sitting still.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Under the Spinning Umbrella. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Sit your child on the chair, holding the seat. Hold the open umbrella low, so it fills the view above the head. Turn it slowly, one turn every four seconds, for 30 seconds. Ask what they feel and write a score from 0 (nothing) to 10 (I am sure I am turning). Then do the same with eyes shut, as a comparison.
flow.say: Hold the chair. Look up at the pattern and keep looking. I will turn the umbrella slowly. Tell me what you feel.
flow.kid: Hold the chair. Look up at the pattern. Say what you feel.
flow.parent: Stay beside the chair. Turn slowly. With two to four children, one sits, one turns, one holds the stopwatch and one writes the scores, and then you rotate. The effect is often weak with a small umbrella, so write the scores honestly. Many children feel that they themselves start to turn, or that the chair tilts, after ten to twenty seconds. Many others feel nothing, and that is a result too. Stop if your child feels sick or dizzy.
flow.context: In this step, you sit under the umbrella while it turns.

flow.do: Swap places. Then ask your child to describe the feeling, and to say which part of the body noticed the turning.
flow.say: Now it is my turn. After this, tell me: was it your eyes, your ears or your feet that told you that you were turning?
flow.kid: Swap. Now you turn the umbrella. Then say what you felt.

check.q: Under a turning umbrella, you may feel that you are turning, though you sit still. Which sense is giving the wrong message?
options: Your eyes
Your feet
Your nose
check.why: Your eyes see the pattern moving across your view. This is what they see when your head turns, so the brain may believe you are turning. Your inner ears and your feet say you are still. The nose does not help with turning, and the feet are giving the right message.

flow.context: In this step, you swap places and think about which sense gave the wrong message.

activities.title: A Fingertip Lighter than a Tomato

materials.item: a digital kitchen scale that reads in grams
a steady table or counter about as high as your child's hip, next to a wall
a small tomato, to feel its weight and weigh it
a phone with a stopwatch
a grown-up who stands beside the child as a spotter
a mat or carpet for the child to stand on, away from stairs

activities.safety: A grown-up stands right beside your child for every try, ready to catch. Use a carpet or a mat, away from stairs, tables with sharp corners and glass. Stop at once if your child feels dizzy.

schedule.what: Weigh the tomato, learn what a light touch feels like, and test standing with no touch, a light touch and a hard push.

activities.record: Write the seconds for each try: no touch, light touch under 100 grams on the scale, and a hard push. Write the weight of your child and of the tomato.
activities.context: In this activity, you stand heel to toe with your eyes shut, and find out whether a touch lighter than a tomato can steady you.

setup.art: A small tomato on a kitchen scale showing about 100 grams.
setup.caption: 1. Weigh a tomato. A force of 1 newton is about its weight.

setup.art: A child standing heel to toe with eyes shut, with one fingertip resting lightly on a kitchen scale on a table, the scale showing 40 grams.
setup.caption: 2. Stand heel to toe, eyes shut. Rest one fingertip on the scale, lighter than the tomato.

setup.art: The same child standing heel to toe with eyes shut, pressing hard on the table with her whole hand, the scale reading a large number.
setup.caption: 3. Try again, pushing hard. Compare the seconds.

flow.do: Weigh the tomato on the scale. Let your child feel how light 100 grams is. Practise touching the scale with one fingertip so that it reads under 100 grams. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: This tomato is about 100 grams. Your fingertip will touch the scale more lightly than that. Do you think a touch that light can help you stand? Why?
flow.kid: A tomato weighs about 100 grams. Touch the scale so lightly that it reads less than 100 grams. Can a touch that light help you stand?

ask.q: Do you think a touch lighter than a tomato will help you stand? Why do you think so?
good: No, it is too light to hold me up.
Yes, because my finger can feel the table.
It will help a little, because I will know where I am.

flow.parent: Switch the scale on and wait for zero before each touch. Practise until your child can keep the reading steady under 100 grams. Do not correct the guess. A kitchen scale costs about Rs 300 to 500. Without one, use a wall: a fingertip touch is light enough if a sheet of paper held between the fingertip and the wall can be pulled out easily. With two to four children, one stands, one watches the scale or the paper, one times, and one writes. Then rotate.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Fingertip Lighter than a Tomato. You weigh a tomato and learn what a very light touch feels like.

flow.do: Your child stands heel to toe on the mat, arms folded, eyes shut. Time two tries with no touch, up to 20 seconds. Then time two tries with one fingertip resting on the scale, under 100 grams.
flow.say: Stand with one foot right in front of the other, and fold your arms. Shut your eyes. Try one, no touch. Try two. Now rest one finger on the scale, very lightly.
flow.kid: Stand heel to toe. Shut your eyes. Try with no touch. Then touch the scale lightly.
flow.parent: Stand close, ready to catch. A try ends when a foot moves or the child opens their eyes. Watch the scale. If the reading goes above 100 grams, it is not a light touch, so repeat the try.
flow.context: In this step, you stand heel to toe with eyes shut, first without touch and then with a very light touch.

flow.do: Do two more tries, leaning on the table with a firm push. Write the seconds. Add up the seconds for each of the three kinds of try.
flow.say: Now push hard on the table with your hand, and try again. Is it steadier than the light touch, or not?
flow.kid: Now push hard on the table. Try again with your eyes shut.
flow.parent: Children are often steadier with both kinds of touch than with none, and about as steady with the light touch as with the hard push. Your result may differ, and that is fine.
flow.context: In this step, you compare the light touch with a hard push.

flow.do: Ask your child what they think happened, what they saw that shows it, and why it happened. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Which was steadier, no touch or light touch? Was the hard push much better? What does the light touch do, if it does not hold you up?
flow.kid: Which was steadiest? Why did a light touch help?

check.q: A touch of less than 100 grams cannot hold up a child who weighs 25 kilograms. Why does it still help?
options: It tells the brain how the body is moving compared with a still object
It takes some of the child's weight
It makes the child's eyes work
check.why: A fingertip on something still gives the brain an extra source of balance information. It is far too light to carry any weight, since 25 kilograms is 25,000 grams, which is 250 times as much. The touch is a message, not a prop.

flow.context: In this step, you explain how such a light touch can help.

activities.title: Warm Hand, Whole Hand: is the same water warmer on more skin?

materials.item: two bowls big enough for a hand
lukewarm water, about 38 degrees Celsius and as warm as a baby's bath, from a warm tap or geyser or mixed from boiled and cold water in a jug, never hotter than 40 degrees Celsius
a kitchen thermometer, if you have one, to check the water
a towel
a phone with a stopwatch
a sheet of paper with a line from 0 to 10 and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up mixes the water, away from the child, and tests it with the inside of their wrist or elbow, as for a baby's bath. Do not carry a hot pan or kettle near the children. The water must be pleasantly warm, never hot, and never hotter than 40 degrees Celsius. Replace the water if it gets cool.

schedule.what: Dip a fingertip, a whole hand and both hands into the same warm water, and give a warmth score each time.

activities.record: For each dip, write the warmth from 0 to 10, where 0 is no warmth and 10 is as warm as is comfortable. Write the water temperature if you measured it.
activities.context: In this activity, you dip a fingertip, a hand and both hands in the same warm water to find out whether the amount of skin changes the feeling.

setup.art: A grown-up testing a bowl of warm water with the inside of her wrist, a kitchen thermometer reading 38 beside the bowl.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up mixes warm water and tests it on the wrist.

setup.art: A child dipping one fingertip into the bowl while a grown-up holds a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Dip one fingertip for 5 seconds. Say the warmth from 0 to 10.

setup.art: The same child with her whole hand in the bowl, and then both hands in two bowls, with a warmth scale beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Dip the whole hand for 5 seconds. Then both hands. Say the warmth each time.

flow.do: A grown-up mixes the warm water and checks it with the wrist, or with a thermometer. Pour it into the two bowls. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Both bowls have the same warm water. If you dip one finger, and then your whole hand, will the warmth feel the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The water is the same. Will a finger and a whole hand feel the same? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a finger and a whole hand might feel different in the same water?
good: More skin means more of me feels the warmth.
The water is the same, so it will feel the same.
A finger is smaller, so it feels less.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Keep the water the same temperature in both bowls. The effect is usually clear but small, so use the score each time, and if all three scores are the same, write that down as a result. Cold hands from a fan or air-conditioner can spoil it, so sit in a normal room for five minutes first. With two to four children, each gives a score on paper, so nobody hears the others' numbers first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Warm Hand, Whole Hand. A grown-up prepares the water, and you guess.

flow.do: Dip one fingertip, up to the first joint, for 5 seconds. Say the warmth from 0 to 10. Dry the hand and rest for a minute. Then dip the whole hand to the wrist for 5 seconds. Say the warmth. Rest. Then dip both hands, one in each bowl, for 5 seconds.
flow.say: Dip one finger for five seconds. How warm, from zero to ten? Dry it. Now your whole hand. Then both hands.
flow.kid: Dip a fingertip for 5 seconds. Say how warm. Then a hand. Then both hands.
flow.parent: Keep each dip to 5 seconds, as the skin soon gets used to the temperature. Rest for a minute between dips. To check whether the order matters, repeat in the opposite order: both hands, whole hand, fingertip.
flow.context: In this step, you dip a fingertip, a hand and both hands, and score the warmth each time.

flow.do: Compare the three scores. Ask your child what they think happened, what they saw that shows it, and why it happened. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Which dip felt warmest? The water was the same each time. So what changed?
flow.kid: Which dip felt warmest? The water did not change. What did?

check.q: The water is the same warmth for a finger and a whole hand. Why can the whole hand feel warmer?
options: More warm gates open at once, and the brain adds up their reports
The water gets hotter when more skin is in it
The finger has no sense of warmth
check.why: A whole hand has far more warm nerve endings in the water than a fingertip. The brain adds their reports. The water has not changed, and the fingertip can sense warmth too. This is called spatial summation.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the scores and explain the result.

activities.title: Count Your Own Heartbeat

materials.item: a phone with a stopwatch
a chair to sit on, in a quiet room
paper and a pencil to write the counts
a grown-up to time and to take the pulse count

activities.safety: The exercise is only 20 star jumps, done on a clear floor. Skip it if your child is unwell. Stop if your child feels dizzy or short of breath. This is not a test of health. Nobody should feel bad about a count that is far off.

schedule.what: Count your heartbeats by feeling only, then by pulse, at rest and after exercise, and compare.

activities.record: A table with four rows: at rest by feeling, at rest by pulse, after exercise by feeling, after exercise by pulse. For each pair, write the difference.
activities.context: In this activity, you count your heartbeats without touching your wrist, and then check by taking your pulse, to see how well a sense that looks inward works.

setup.art: A child sitting quietly on a chair with her eyes closed and her hands on her knees, a phone stopwatch on the table.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still and quiet. Count the beats you can feel, for 30 seconds.

setup.art: The same child with two fingers on her wrist while a grown-up holds a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Now count your pulse with your fingers, for 30 seconds.

setup.art: The child doing star jumps, then sitting again with a hand on her chest.
setup.caption: 3. Do 20 star jumps. Sit and count again, both ways.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Sit your child quietly for one minute, eyes closed, hands on the knees.
flow.say: Sit still and be quiet for a minute. Can you feel your heart beating anywhere? Do you think you could count the beats without touching your wrist? Why?
flow.kid: Sit still. Can you feel your heart? Could you count the beats?

ask.q: Where in your body do you think you might feel your heart?
good: In my chest.
In my ears or neck.
In my fingers, if they are still.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children feel the heartbeat in the chest, the neck or the fingertips. Some feel nothing at rest, and that is common.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count Your Own Heartbeat. You sit quietly and guess.

flow.do: Time 30 seconds. Your child counts the beats they can feel without touching a wrist or neck, and says the number. Then time 30 seconds more. Your child finds the pulse at the wrist, and counts the beats with their fingers. Write both numbers.
flow.say: Count the beats you can feel inside, without using your fingers. I will time thirty seconds. Now find the pulse on your wrist, and count again.
flow.kid: Count the beats you feel inside for 30 seconds. Then count your pulse with your fingers.
flow.parent: If your child feels no heartbeat, write 0 and say so. Do not make up a number, because that spoils the result. A count that is far from the pulse is common. Hold two fingers, not the thumb, on the wrist below the thumb.
flow.context: In this step, you count your heartbeat by feeling and by pulse, while sitting still.

flow.do: Your child does 20 star jumps and sits down at once, because the heart slows within a minute. Repeat both counts for 30 seconds each. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Do twenty star jumps, then sit. Count again by feeling, then by pulse. Is it easier now to feel your heart?
flow.kid: Do 20 star jumps. Sit. Count your beats both ways again.
flow.parent: After exercise the heart beats harder and faster, so many people can count it more accurately. The count by feeling is often smaller than the pulse count. The heart slows a little during the minute, so the second count is a bit low. Always do the feeling count first, at rest and after exercise, so the comparison is fair. Pairs work well: one child counts and the other times, then swap, and each child can also take the other's pulse.
flow.context: In this step, you do some exercise and then repeat both counts.

flow.do: Subtract each pair of counts. Ask which was closer, rest or exercise. Ask the check question.
flow.say: How close were you at rest? How close after the star jumps? Why do you think it was easier after the star jumps?
flow.kid: Compare your counts. When were you closest? Why?

check.q: Many people count their heartbeat more accurately after exercise. Why?
options: Each beat is stronger, so the inside sensors report it more clearly
The heart stops beating when you are resting
The wrist pulse gets easier to hear
check.why: After exercise the heart pumps harder, so the signals from the chest and blood vessels are stronger and easier to notice. The heart never stops at rest. The pulse at the wrist is the same kind of beat before and after.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the counts and explain the result.

activities.title: Matka Magic: how does sweat cool you?

materials.item: two identical steel tumblers or two identical glass jars
a clean cotton cloth, cut into two equal pieces big enough to wrap round a tumbler, and two rubber bands
warm water, about 40 degrees Celsius, from a warm tap or geyser or mixed from boiled and cold water in a jug, never hotter than 40 degrees Celsius
a thermometer that reads between 30 and 45 degrees: a kitchen thermometer, or a digital fever thermometer from a medical shop (about Rs 100 to 200)
a table fan, or a breezy window
a phone with a timer, and paper and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up fills the tumblers with warm water, away from the child, and checks it with the wrist, as for a baby's bath. The water must never be hotter than 40 degrees Celsius. Keep the fan, the plug and the wires away from the water.

schedule.what: Wrap one tumbler in a wet cloth and one in a dry cloth, fill both with the same warm water, and put them in front of a fan for 15 minutes.

activities.record: Write the starting temperature of each tumbler and the temperature after 15 minutes. Work out how much each one cooled. Write the temperature of the room.
activities.context: In this activity, you cool warm water with a wet cloth and a fan, to see how the sweat on your skin helps keep you cool.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers on a table, one wrapped in a dripping wet cloth and one in a dry cloth, both held by rubber bands.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap one tumbler in a wet cloth and one in a dry cloth.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring warm water into both tumblers, and a thermometer in one of them showing 38.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up fills both with the same warm water. Measure each.

setup.art: Two tumblers side by side in front of a table fan, a phone timer set to 15 minutes beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Put them in front of the fan for 15 minutes.

setup.art: A thermometer in each tumbler in turn, and a child writing numbers in a table.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the water again and work out how much each cooled.

flow.do: Show your child both tumblers and the cloths. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: One cloth will be wet and one dry. Both tumblers hold the same warm water, in front of a fan. Which will cool more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One cloth is wet. One is dry. Which tumbler cools more? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the wet cloth might cool the water more, or less?
good: Water drying takes heat away.
The wet cloth covers the steel and keeps the heat in.
A wet cloth is cold, so it cools the water.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A matka, a clay water pot, keeps water cool in the same way.
flow.context: This is the first step of Matka Magic. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Wet one cloth with tap water and wring it so that it does not drip. Wrap it round one tumbler with a rubber band. Wrap the dry cloth round the other. A grown-up fills both with warm water. Measure the temperature of each with the thermometer and write it down.
flow.say: Wrap the wet cloth round this tumbler and the dry cloth round the other. Now we fill both with the same warm water. What does the thermometer say?
flow.kid: Wrap a wet cloth round one tumbler. Wrap a dry cloth round the other. Measure the water.
flow.parent: Wring the wet cloth well. The start temperatures should be almost the same. Fill the tumblers within a minute of each other. If you have only a fever thermometer, use water between 35 and 42 degrees.
flow.context: In this step, you prepare both tumblers and measure their starting temperatures.

flow.do: Put the tumblers side by side in front of the fan. Start a timer for 15 minutes. While you wait, talk about when you feel cool in a breeze after swimming or sweating.
flow.say: While we wait, think. When do you feel cold in a breeze? What is on your skin then?
flow.kid: Put the tumblers in the breeze. Wait 15 minutes. Think about sweat.
flow.wait: Leave the tumblers in front of the fan for 15 minutes.
flow.parent: On a very humid day, such as in Chennai during the monsoon, the difference may be small. A table fan helps a lot. Do not touch the tumblers during the wait. Typical result: the wet cloth cools the water a few degrees more in 15 minutes, but the numbers depend on the weather. In a hot room the water may not cool much at all, so also compare how the two feel. If the fever thermometer shows Lo, write under 32. With two to four children, one measures each tumbler, one writes and one watches the clock. Repeat with the cloths swapped, so the test is fair to both tumblers.
flow.context: In this step, you leave the tumblers in the breeze and wait.

flow.do: Measure each tumbler again. Subtract to find how much each cooled. Compare the two. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which tumbler cooled more? By how many degrees? Water on the cloth dried. What did it take with it?
flow.kid: Measure again. Which tumbler cooled more? By how much?

check.q: The tumbler with the wet cloth cooled more than the one with the dry cloth. What took the extra heat away?
options: Water drying off the cloth took heat with it
The wet cloth was colder than the dry cloth
The fan blew cold air onto the wet cloth only
check.why: When water dries into the air, it takes heat from the thing it dries from. This is why wet things cool in a breeze, and why sweat cools your skin. The fan blew on both tumblers equally, and the two cloths started at nearly the same warmth.

flow.context: In this step, you measure again and explain what cooled the water.

activities.title: Be a Pit Viper: find the warm cup with your eyes shut

materials.item: three identical steel tumblers
warm water, as warm as a baby's bath and never hotter than 40 degrees Celsius, for one tumbler (from a warm tap or geyser, or boiled and cold water mixed in a jug)
room-temperature tap water for the other two tumblers (or water chilled in the fridge, if the weather is hot)
a tea towel to dry the outsides of the tumblers
a scarf or a sleep mask, or just closed eyes
paper and a pencil to write the score

activities.safety: A grown-up fills the tumblers away from the child and tests the warm one with the inside of the wrist, as for a baby's bath. The warm water must never be hotter than 40 degrees Celsius. The child never touches the tumblers during the test. Keep the room quiet, and replace the warm water when it cools.

schedule.what: Guess, then play 12 rounds of finding the warm tumbler by feeling its warmth with your cheek, and count the right answers.

activities.record: Write a tick for each round you got right, out of 12. Write how far from the tumbler your cheek was. Write the number of right answers you would expect by luck.
activities.context: In this activity, you play a snake that hunts by heat, and try to find a warm tumbler among three with your eyes shut.

setup.art: Three identical steel tumblers in a row on a table, one with a small red steam curl drawn above it.
setup.caption: 1. Fill one tumbler with warm water and two with tap water.

setup.art: A child with closed eyes holding her cheek about 5 centimetres from the middle tumbler, a grown-up watching quietly.
setup.caption: 2. With eyes shut, hold your cheek close to each tumbler. Do not touch.

setup.art: The child pointing at one tumbler and a grown-up making a tick on a score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Point to the warm one. The grown-up checks and ticks.

flow.do: Show your child the three tumblers. Ask for a guess and a reason. Ask how many of 12 they would get right by pure luck.
flow.say: One tumbler is warm and two are not. They look the same. With your eyes shut, can you find the warm one without touching? How many of twelve would you get right by luck alone?
flow.kid: One cup is warm. Two are not. Can you find it with your eyes shut?

ask.q: How many of 12 rounds would you get right by luck alone, and why?
good: Four, because there are three cups and one is right.
A third of them, which is four.
About four, because one in three is the warm cup.

flow.parent: By luck, one in three would be right, which is 4 of 12. Any score well above 4 would suggest the child really feels the warmth.
flow.context: This is the first step of Be a Pit Viper. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up fills one tumbler with warm water and two with tap water. Dry the outsides. Put them in a row. Cover your child's eyes.
flow.say: Close your eyes. I will shuffle the cups. Do not touch them. Hold your cheek close to each one, like a snake feeling for a warm mouse.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Do not touch the cups.
flow.parent: Handle all three tumblers the same way, so no tumbler is warmed by hands. The child playing the viper must breathe out away from the tumblers, since breath is warm. With two to four children, one is the viper, one shuffles, and one records, and then you rotate. Each viper plays 12 rounds. Do not let the child hear or see the shuffling. Move the cups smoothly and quietly. Dry the outsides so that no wet marks give a clue.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up prepares the three tumblers and the child covers their eyes.

flow.do: Play 12 rounds. Each round, shuffle the tumblers. Your child holds a cheek about 5 centimetres from each one in turn, not touching, and points to the warmest. Tick if right. Refill with warm water after six rounds. Then try 10 centimetres away for six more rounds.
flow.say: Hold your cheek near the first cup. Now the second. Now the third. Which feels warmest? Point.
flow.kid: Hold your cheek near each cup. Point to the warmest. Do not touch.
flow.parent: Many children can find the warm cup from 5 centimetres. At 10 centimetres it becomes much harder. Write down where it stops working. In hot weather, when the room and tap water are already warm, scores may stay near 4, so chill the two cold tumblers in the fridge. The warm tumbler cools, so refill it after six rounds.
flow.context: In this step, you play twelve rounds and count how many you get right.

flow.do: Count the right answers. Compare them with the 4 you would get by luck. Ask the check question.
flow.say: How many did you get right? Luck would give about four. What does your score say? What does a snake have that you do not?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Is it more than 4? What does that tell you?

check.q: Suppose you got 9 of 12 right. By luck you would expect 4. What does this suggest?
options: You really can feel warmth at a distance
The cups were noisy
Luck cannot be counted
check.why: A score far above what luck gives suggests that your skin picked up the warmth coming off the tumbler. A snake's pit does the same job much better. The cups were not noisy, since the child kept quiet and still, and luck can be counted: one in three.

flow.context: In this step, you compare your score with luck and think about what it means.

projects.title: Family Balance Lab: three days, eight people

materials.item: the blanket, the stopwatch and the clear space from the Balance Team test
a sheet of paper ruled into a table with a row for each person and a column for each of four tests
a pencil and a ruler to draw the bars
a sturdy chair or a counter for each person to hold, if they want to

projects.safety: Ask each person if they would like to take part, and never push anyone. Older people, and people who feel unsteady, should do the tests close to a chair or counter they can hold, and should skip any test that feels unsafe. A grown-up stands beside everyone doing a test. Stop if anyone feels dizzy.

schedule.what: Test two or three people with the four tests from the Balance Team test.
Test two or three more people. Write every result in the table.
Add up, find the average for each test, draw a bar chart and discuss what you found.

projects.record: A table with a row for each person and four columns for the tests. Then a row for the average of each test, and a bar chart of the four averages.
projects.context: In this project, you test eight people with the four Balance Team tests and look for a pattern across the group.

setup.art: A table ruled on paper with names of family members down the left and four test names across the top.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the table, with a row for each person.

setup.art: A grandmother standing near a counter, holding the counter lightly with one hand, a child timing her with a phone while an adult stands close.
setup.caption: 2. Test each person who agrees to take part, close to a counter.

setup.art: A bar chart on paper with four bars, one for each test, and a child colouring the longest bar.
setup.caption: 3. Find the average for each test and draw four bars.

flow.do: Choose eight people who agree to take part, such as family, neighbours and friends. If you cannot find eight, five is enough. Today test two or three of them. Each person does the four tests on one foot, close to a chair or counter. Give one try per test. Time up to 30 seconds. Write the seconds in the table. Change the order of the tests for each person, so that tiredness affects every test equally.
flow.say: We are going to test eight people with the four balance tests. Ask each person if they would like to try. Nobody has to. We write down all the seconds.
flow.kid: Ask people if they want to try. Time each person in the four tests.

ask.q: Do you think the same test will be the hardest for everyone? Why?
good: Yes, because everyone has the same three helpers.
No, because some people use their eyes more than others.
Maybe older people will find it harder.

flow.parent: People over 60, and anyone who feels unsteady, should do the eyes-open tests on the bare floor only, and hold a counter with one hand. They should skip the blanket and the eyes-shut tests. In the average, count only the people who did that test. One child works with a parent. With two to four children, one is the spotter, one times, and one writes in the table. Do not let anyone do a test that makes them anxious. Write down what each person says about how it felt.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Family Balance Lab. You test your first people.

flow.do: Test more people. Write the seconds in the table. Notice which test is hardest for each person, and whether it is the same for everyone.
flow.say: Today we test more people. Which test is hardest for each person? Is it the same one for everyone?
flow.kid: Test more people. Write the seconds. Which test is hardest?
flow.wait: Test two or three more people on day 2.
flow.context: This is the second day of the Family Balance Lab. You test more people.

flow.do: Add the seconds for each test, and divide by the number of people to find the average. Draw four bars. Discuss what you found, and ask the check question.
flow.say: Add up each column. Divide by the number of people. Draw a bar for each average. Which is the lowest bar? Is it the test you expected?
flow.kid: Add each column. Divide by the number of people. Draw the bars.

check.q: Why is an average of eight people more trustworthy than the result of one person?
options: One person's result can be a fluke, and an average smooths flukes out
Eight people always give the same result
An average makes the tests easier
check.why: One try can be lucky or unlucky. An average of many people shows the pattern that most people share. Eight people do not always give the same result, and an average does not change how hard a test is.

flow.context: This is the last day of the Family Balance Lab. You find averages and draw the pattern.

challenges.title: Night Path for Paati: help a grandparent walk safely in the dark
challenges.safety: This is a model path in a room, tested by a child with a grown-up beside. Keep the floor clear. Use a torch or a plug-in night light, never a candle or a lamp with a flame. Nothing is stuck on a floor where a real grandparent walks until a grown-up has checked that it cannot slip or trip anyone. Walk slowly, with a grown-up's hand ready.
challenges.problem: A grandparent feels unsteady in the dark. Their feet tell them less than they used to. They need to walk from the bed to the toilet at night, without waking anyone and without falling. Design a night path that gives all three balance helpers, and a touch helper, what they need.
constraints: It must cost very little and be easy to make at home.
It must have no flame, no loose wires and nothing to trip on.
It must work for someone who does not want to lean on anything.
It must be easy for the grandparent to understand without reading.
materials: a torch or a low night light
strips of rough cloth or cloth tape
a chair, to stand for a bed, and a table, to stand for the toilet door
general: A low night light that lights the floor, not the eyes, so the eyes can see where to step.
A firm handrail along the wall at hand height, to touch lightly.
A non-slip mat at the start and end of the path, with edges that are stuck down.
creative: A strip of rough cloth stuck along the wall at hand height, so a fingertip can follow it like a guide, even in total darkness.
A change in how the floor feels, such as a ridged mat placed one step before each turn, so the feet get a message before the eyes need one.
A walking stick kept by the bed, with a bright tip, for touching the floor lightly as a sensor.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your path from the bed to the toilet. Mark where each balance helper is helped. Test it with the lights off and a grown-up beside you, and write what you would change.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the balance team. You design a path that helps someone whose feet no longer tell them as much as before.

setup.art: A child's plan of a bedroom, passage and bathroom with symbols for a night light, a wall strip, a mat and a stick.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a plan of the path, from the bed to the toilet.

setup.art: A passage with rough cloth stuck along the wall at hand height and a low light on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Add a wall strip to touch and a low light.

setup.art: A child walking the path with the lights off, a torch low in one hand, a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Test it in the dark with a grown-up beside you.

flow.do: Read the problem together. List the dangers on the path, and which balance helpers are weak in the dark. Ask your child to draw two ideas.
flow.say: In the dark, the eyes help little, and tired feet tell less. What can we add so that someone walking has more help? Draw two ideas.
flow.kid: Think of dangers in a dark passage. Draw two ideas.

ask.q: Which helper does each of your ideas help: the eyes, the feet, or a light touch?
good: A night light helps the eyes.
A wall strip helps the fingertip.
A ridged mat tells the feet where to turn.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Night Path challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Choose the best idea. Build it from paper, cloth and cardboard on a model path in the room. Use a chair for the bed and a table for the toilet door. Mark where each helper is helped.
flow.say: Pick your best idea and build it. Label each part with the helper it helps: eyes, feet or touch.
flow.kid: Build your best idea. Label each part with the helper it helps.
flow.parent: Keep everything on the floor flat and stuck down. Nothing should block the path or be a tripping hazard. Avoid candles, oil lamps and loose wires.
flow.context: In this step, you build the path from simple materials and label each part.

flow.do: Switch the lights off. With a grown-up beside you and a torch held low, walk your path. Write what worked, what did not, and one thing to change.
flow.say: Lights off. I will walk beside you. Does your path help your eyes, your feet and your fingertip? What would you change?
flow.kid: Lights off. Walk the path with a grown-up. What would you change?
flow.parent: Hold your child's hand if they feel unsteady. The aim is to see which helpers the path supports.
flow.context: In this step, you test the path with the lights off.

challenges.title: Heat Cloak: hide a warm tumbler from a pit viper
challenges.problem: In Be a Pit Viper, a child with eyes shut finds a warm tumbler by the warmth coming off the outside of the tumbler. Make a cover that hides the warm tumbler from a classmate who is playing the pit viper, with their cheek 5 centimetres away. The viper should not be able to find the tumbler better than by luck.
constraints: The warm tumbler must hold warm water, never hotter than 40 degrees Celsius.
The cover must be made only from kitchen and craft things, and must fit round the tumbler.
The pit viper may not touch the tumbler or the cover, and must keep their eyes shut.
You have 12 rounds, as in Be a Pit Viper, to test your cover.
materials: warm water, never hotter than 40 degrees Celsius

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT one of the three sources of information the brain mixes to balance?
opts: The nose
The inner ears
The eyes
The feet and muscles
quiz.why: Balance uses sight, the inner ears, and the sensors in the feet and muscles. The nose smells and does not help you know whether you are upright.

quiz.p: A child stands on a thick mattress with her eyes shut and wobbles a lot. What is the best explanation?
opts: Two helpers are weak, so only her inner ears are working clearly
Her inner ears have stopped working
The mattress makes her heavier
quiz.why: With her eyes shut there is no sight, and the soft mattress makes the signals from her feet unclear. The inner ears still work, but they cannot do the whole job alone.

quiz.p: What makes it possible to read a sign while your head bobs in a bumpy bus?
opts: The head-turn reflex, which moves the eyes opposite to the head
The sign moves with your head
Your eyes follow the sign on purpose very quickly
quiz.why: The inner ear senses the head moving and starts a very fast reflex that moves the eyes the other way. Following the sign on purpose is much too slow to do this.

quiz.p: The train beside yours starts to move, and you feel yours slide backwards. Which sense gave the wrong message?
opts: Your eyes
Your inner ears
Your feet
quiz.why: Your eyes saw a moving picture, which is what you see when you move yourself. Your inner ears and feet correctly said you were still.

quiz.p: Why can a very light fingertip on a wall steady a person?
opts: It gives the brain more information about how the body is moving
It takes weight off the feet
It stops the inner ears from swirling
quiz.why: A still wall tells the brain how the body is swaying, even though the force is far too small to hold anyone up. The touch is a message, not a prop.

quiz.p: Why does a green chilli feel hot, though the chilli is not warm?
opts: It opens the same gate in your nerve endings that heat opens
The chilli is secretly boiling
The tongue cannot tell hot from cold
quiz.why: Capsaicin, the chemical in chilli, opens the same gate that warm temperatures open. The nerve then sends a signal that means hot. The chilli's temperature does not change.

quiz.p: What happens in the body's temperature loop when you get too warm?
opts: Sensors tell the brain, and the body sweats and widens the skin's blood vessels
The brain stops measuring
The body shivers to make heat
quiz.why: The loop senses the warmth, then acts to cool the body. Sweat dries and takes heat away, and wider blood vessels let heat leave the skin. Shivering is the response to being too cool.

quiz.p: When you stub your toe, you feel a sharp jab and then a throb. Why are there two kinds of pain?
opts: The signals travel along two kinds of nerve fibre at different speeds
Your toe gets hurt twice
Your brain forgets and remembers the pain
quiz.why: The fast fibres carry a sharp signal, and the slow fibres carry a dull throbbing one. The throb arrives later because its fibres are thinner and have no fast coat.

quiz.p: A person is distracted by an exciting game and does not notice a scraped knee until the game ends. What does this suggest?
opts: Attention changes how strongly pain is felt
The scrape was not real
The nerves in the knee stopped working
quiz.why: The brain weighs pain against everything else it is paying attention to. The scrape was real, and the nerves worked, but the pain was turned down while the mind was busy.

quiz.p: What do the halteres of a fly do?
opts: They swing and sense when the body turns
They help the fly smell
They make the fly's buzzing sound
quiz.why: The halteres swing as the wings beat. When the body turns, the swinging clubs are pushed sideways, and sensors at the base feel that push.

quiz.p: A pit viper has the same kind of gate that other animals use for pain. What does this suggest about how new senses begin?
opts: Evolution often tunes an old gate to a new job
Evolution builds every sense from nothing
Snakes copy the senses of other animals
quiz.why: In snakes and bats, the heat sense uses gates related to ones in other animals, tuned to different temperatures. Evolution often reuses what it has.

quiz.p: To test whether a soft surface changes balance, a child stands on a blanket on one try and on a floor on the next. What else must stay the same for a fair test?
opts: The pose, the foot, the eyes and the rest between tries
The colour of the blanket
Nothing, because only the surface matters
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If the eyes were open on one try and shut on another, you could not tell whether the surface or the eyes made the difference.

items.p: Which three sources of information does the brain mix to know whether you are upright?
opts: Eyes, inner ears, and sensors in the feet and muscles
Nose, tongue and skin
Eyes, nose and ears
items.why: Your eyes show where the horizon and the floor are. Your inner ears feel turning, tilting and speeding up. The sensors in your feet and muscles feel the ground and your joints. Smell and taste do not help you balance.

items.p: The three liquid-filled loops in each inner ear that feel turning are called the semicircular ____.
items.why: When your head turns, the liquid in the canals lags behind and bends tiny hairs. The hairs send signals to the brain.

items.p: Match each source of balance information to what it tells the brain.
pairs: Eyes
where the horizon and the walls are
Semicircular canals
that the head is turning
Ear crystals
which way is down, and when you speed up
Sensors in the feet and muscles
what the ground is like, and how the joints are bent
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each source gives the brain a different kind of message, and the brain mixes them. None of them gives the whole picture.

items.p: Standing on a soft blanket with your eyes shut weakens two of your three balance helpers.
items.why: True. Shutting the eyes takes away the information from sight. The soft blanket makes the signals from the feet and ankles less clear. Only the inner ears are left clear, so most people wobble a lot.

items.p: Sort these moments by the balance helper that is weak, missing or fooled.
items: a dark room with no light at all
the room seems to turn after you spin
the train beside yours seems to move yours
a foot that has fallen asleep
items.a: see items
items.why: In the dark, the eyes give no information. After spinning, the liquid in the canals keeps moving, so the ears are fooled. On sand and in a numb foot, the feet give unclear messages. In space, the crystals cannot tell which way is down.

items.p: In the Balance Team test, standing on the blanket with eyes shut gave the shortest time. Explain why, using the words 'helpers' and 'inner ears'.
items.a: With my eyes shut, my eyes gave no information. The soft blanket made the signals from my feet unclear. So two helpers were weak, and only my inner ears were left to tell my brain how I was standing. That is why I wobbled most.
items.why: A strong answer says that two helpers were weakened at once, and that the third could not do the job alone. It does not say that the eyes or the blanket caused the wobble by themselves.

items.p: Draw a child's head and body. Draw three lines that carry messages to the brain from the eyes, the inner ears and the feet. Label each line with what it tells the brain.
items.a: A child with three lines going to the head: from the eyes (where the horizon is), from the ears (turning and tilting), and from the feet (what the ground is like).
items.why: Balance is not one sense in one place. It is three sources of information that the brain mixes.

items.p: What does the head-turn reflex do?
opts: Moves your eyes the opposite way to your head, so what you look at stays steady
Turns your head when your eyes move
Makes you dizzy when you turn quickly
items.why: When your head turns, the inner ear starts a very quick eye movement the other way. This keeps the picture on your eye steady. Dizziness comes from the same reflex after spinning, but it is not the job of the reflex.

items.p: Put these in order: what happens when you shake your head while reading.
items: your eyes swing the opposite way
the liquid in a canal lags behind and bends tiny hairs
the print stays steady on your eye
a: the liquid in a canal lags behind and bends tiny hairs
your eyes swing the opposite way
the print stays steady on your eye
items.why: The turn of the head moves the liquid in a canal, the hairs send a signal, and the signal swings the eyes the other way within about a hundredth of a second.

items.p: Label the parts of the fly: wings, halteres, legs.
items.why: The halteres are the tiny club-shaped stalks behind the wings. They swing as the wings beat, and they sense when the body turns.
items.art: A fly seen from above with three blank label lines pointing at the wings, the two tiny knobbed stalks behind them, and the legs.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Halteres, ear crystals, semicircular canals, heat pits.
items.a: heat pits
items.why: Halteres, ear crystals and semicircular canals all help an animal sense turning, tilting or speeding up. Heat pits sense warmth from a distance.

items.p: A fingertip rests on a still wall with a force too light to hold a person up. Why does it still steady them?
opts: It gives the brain extra information about how the body is moving
It takes some of their weight
It makes the floor firmer
items.why: A still wall under a fingertip tells the brain exactly how the body is moving compared with the room. The force is much too small to carry weight. The touch works as a sense, not as a prop.

items.p: A fever means the body has lost control of its temperature.
items.why: False. In a fever, the brain's thermostat is set higher on purpose, so the body shivers until it reaches the higher number. The control loop is working, though a very high or long fever needs a doctor.

items.p: Rubbing a bumped elbow helps because touch signals compete with ____ signals.
items.why: Touch signals travel quickly and can turn down the pain signals at the spinal cord. Scientists have changed the details of this idea since 1965, but rubbing a bump does help.

items.p: Anitha and her grandmother are choosing a walking stick. Her grandmother says a stick shows she is weak.

views.says: A stick is a prop for weak people. I will manage without one.
A stick you only touch lightly is a sensor. It tells your feet where the ground is.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what happens when a fingertip rests lightly on a still wall: the person stands steadier. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Anitha, because light touch gives the brain extra balance information even when it carries no weight. It also says that Grandmother is right that a stick can be used as a prop, to take weight off a sore knee, and that this is a different use.
items.why: The light touch of a stick or a finger works as a fourth source of balance information. A prop is a different use.

items.p: When the eyes are shut, the brain relies more on the inner ears and the feet. What is this called?
opts: Reweighting
Reflecting
Dizziness
items.why: Reweighting means listening more to the senses that work well and less to those that do not. The brain does this without you choosing.

items.p: A child reads a comic in a bus on a winding road and feels sick. Which pair of senses give messages that do not match?
opts: Her eyes say still, and her inner ears say moving
Her nose says still, and her tongue says moving
Her eyes and her ears both say moving
items.why: The comic is still in her hands, so her eyes see no movement. Her inner ears feel every turn and bump. When these two disagree, the brain is confused. Looking at the horizon makes the messages agree again.

items.p: A fly keeps her balance with two tiny club-shaped stalks called ____.
items.why: The halteres swing up and down as the wings beat, and sensors at their base feel when the body turns. A fly without them cannot fly steadily.

items.p: Match each animal to the sense that solves a problem in their life.
pairs: Fly
halteres that feel turning
Python
heat pits that sense a warm animal
Fish
ear stones that sense tilting and record age
Mosquito
a nose for carbon dioxide and heat
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each animal has a sense for a problem in their own life. A fly must steer in the air, a python hunts at night, a fish must know which way is up, and a mosquito must find blood.

items.p: Sort these by the gate in the skin that they open.
items: a hot tawa near the hand
items.a: see items
items.why: The heat gate opens above about 43 degrees and for chilli. The cool gate opens below about 26 degrees and for menthol, the chemical in mint.

items.p: When you dip more of your hand into the same warm water, the water itself gets warmer.
items.why: False. The water stays the same. A bigger area of skin opens more warm gates, and the brain adds their reports, so the same water feels warmer. This is called spatial summation.

items.p: Explain why sweat cools you down. Use the words 'dries' and 'heat'.
items.a: When sweat dries off my skin, it takes heat with it. So my skin and the blood under it cool down. That is how my body gets rid of extra heat.
items.why: A strong answer says that water carries heat away when it dries. This is also why, in Matka Magic, the tumbler with the wet cloth cooled more than the one with the dry cloth.

items.p: Draw a loop of four arrows that shows how the body keeps its temperature steady when you get too warm. Label each arrow.
items.a: A loop: sensors in the skin and body feel the warmth, the brain compares it with the level it aims for, the body sweats and widens its skin blood vessels, and the temperature falls and is sensed again.
items.why: A feedback loop senses, compares, acts and checks again. Sensing is only half of the loop. The other half is the action it triggers.

items.p: Put these in order: what happens when the brain raises the level the body aims for, in a fever.
items: the brain's thermostat is set higher
a: the brain's thermostat is set higher
items.why: At first the body is cooler than the new level, so you feel cold and shiver to make heat. The temperature then climbs until it reaches the higher level.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Shivering, goosebumps, narrowing the blood vessels of the skin, sweating.
items.a: sweating
items.why: Shivering, goosebumps and narrowing the skin's blood vessels all help the body keep or make heat. Sweating cools the body down.

items.p: Two children, Mina and Revathi, talk about pain after one of them scrapes a knee.

views.says: Pain is a sense, like seeing. Special nerve endings catch harm, and the feeling is what their signal feels like.
The signal is not yet pain. The brain builds pain from the signal, from fear and from attention, so the same scrape can hurt a lot or a little.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what happened in Ice in the Palm, when you held the ice cube and only watched it, and when you held it and counted backwards. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer may agree with Revathi, because the same ice cube gave a different ache when the mind was busy. It can also say that Mina is right that special nerve endings catch harm, so the signal is real. Scientists still argue about which view is better.
items.why: This is a question that scientists still debate. Both views fit some of the evidence.

items.p: A child weighs 25 kilograms. A fingertip touch on a wall has a force of about 100 grams. About how many times heavier is the child than the touch?
opts: 250 times
25 times
2,500 times
items.why: 25 kilograms is 25,000 grams. 25,000 divided by 100 is 250. So the touch is about 250 times too small to hold the child up, and yet it steadies them.

items.p: Label the parts of the pit viper's head: eye, nostril, heat pit.
items.why: The heat pit sits between the eye and the nostril. A thin skin inside it warms up when a warm animal is near.
items.art: The head of a pit viper from the side with three blank label lines pointing at the eye, the nostril, and the small pit between them.

items.p: An astronaut floating in a space station gets the usual message from her ear crystals about which way is down.
items.why: False. In free fall the ear crystals do not press down on their jelly, so they cannot say which way is down. Many astronauts feel sick for the first days until the brain adjusts.

items.p: In the Shake the Head or Shake the Page test, why was it easier to read with a shaking head than with a shaking page?
items.a: When my head shakes, my inner ears start the head-turn reflex and move my eyes the opposite way almost at once. When the page shakes, my eyes must follow it on purpose, which is much slower, so the print smears.
items.why: A strong answer says that the reflex is automatic and very fast, and that following on purpose is slow.

items.p: Scientists count the layers in a fish's ear stone. What do the layers tell them?
opts: How old the fish is, because the stone grows a layer at a time
How fast the fish can swim
What the fish ate yesterday
items.why: An ear stone grows a thin new layer every day, and thicker layers in good seasons, so the count shows the age. The stone does not tell speed or meals.

worksheets.title: Test It, Weigh It, Argue It (challenge)

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether the soles of your feet matter for balance. Say what you will change, what you will keep the same, and what you will measure.
items.a: Stand on one foot on a thick towel and on the bare floor, with the same pose, the same foot and my eyes open. Keep the room, the timer and the rest between tries the same. Measure the seconds until the foot touches down. I would change only the surface.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps the others the same, and measures with a number. It also repeats the tries, because one try can be luck.

items.p: A child stands on one foot for the full 30 seconds in every one of her four balance tests. What should she do to learn something from the test?
opts: Make the pose harder, so the tests give different times
Stop, because the test does not work
Say that her balance is perfect
items.why: When every result hits the top time, the test cannot tell the conditions apart. Making the pose harder, such as heel to toe, spreads the results out. This is part of designing a good test.

items.p: Two friends, Jaya and Sudha, are told to 'stand still' on one foot.

views.says: To stay balanced, you should hold your body as still as a statue.
A balanced body is always moving a little. It sways and corrects, again and again.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you know about the three helpers. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Sudha, because the brain keeps correcting small sways using eyes, ears and feet. It can say that Jaya is right that big wobbling is not helpful, and that calm, small movements look still.
items.why: Standing still is work. A stiff body corrects less well, and a body that moves a little all the time is the steadier one.

items.p: In a room where the walls slide forward but the floor stays still, a toddler leans back. What is the best explanation?
opts: Her eyes say she is moving forward, and she corrects for it
Her feet feel the walls moving
Her ears feel the floor sliding
items.why: The eyes see the room sliding, which is how it looks when you move forward. The brain believes the eyes for a moment and leans back. The feet and ears are not fooled, and the floor does not move.

items.p: The feeling that you are moving, when only the world you see is moving, is called ____.
items.why: Vection is the train illusion. The eyes report movement and the brain may believe them, even though the ears and seat say you are still.

items.p: Sort each result into the idea it supports.
cats: Pain is built by the brain
items: eyes shut on a blanket wobbled most
a wounded soldier asked for little pain medicine
Pain is built by the brain
the next train made mine seem to move
a light fingertip steadied a whole body
counting backwards lowered the ache of ice
Pain is built by the brain
a turning umbrella made me feel I was turning
items.a: see items
items.why: Each result shows one idea. Taking helpers away or adding one shows the team. A change of pain with attention shows that the brain builds pain. A moving picture that moves you shows that senses can be fooled.

items.p: Pythons and pit vipers have heat pits. A vampire bat has a heat sense in her nose. All of them use a gate that other animals use for pain or heat. What does this suggest about how evolution makes new senses?
items.a: It suggests that evolution often takes a gate that already exists, such as the ones for heat or pain, and tunes it to a new job, instead of building something brand new each time.
items.why: In snakes and bats, the heat gates are versions of gates found in other animals. They are tuned to open at different temperatures.

items.p: Draw your family's night path to the toilet. Mark with arrows where the eyes, the feet and a light fingertip get help.
items.a: A plan of the path with a low light for the eyes, a rough strip or handrail for the fingertip, and a firm mat or ridged floor for the feet.
items.why: A good design gives each of the balance helpers something to work with, even when the eyes can see little.

items.p: In Be a Pit Viper, 9 of 12 guesses were right, while luck would give 4. What can you say?
opts: The result is well above luck, so the skin probably did sense the warm cup
The result is luck, because anything can happen
The experiment was spoiled
items.why: Four of twelve is what you would expect from random guessing among three cups. Nine of twelve is much higher. We cannot be completely sure from one test, but it is good evidence that the warmth was sensed.

items.p: If two tests give the same answer, it means one of the tests was done wrongly.
items.why: False. Sometimes two things really do make the same difference, or a difference is too small to see. A result that does not change is still a result, and should be written down.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Reading a still book in a moving car, a spinning umbrella above a still chair, a lift moving at steady speed, a film of a roller coaster.
items.a: a lift moving at steady speed
items.why: In the other three, the eyes and the inner ears give messages that do not match. In a steady lift, nothing is fooled. The ears simply feel no change.

items.p: Two scientists look at the pit of a pit viper.

views.says: The pit is a new sense, because no other animal has one.
The pit uses an old gate that other animals use for pain. It is an old gate with a new job.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you know about the snake's heat gate and the chilli gate. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Dr Ali that the pit uses a gate that other animals use for other jobs. It can say that Dr Rao is right that the snake gains a sense that most animals lack, so the pit does work as a new sense.
items.why: Both views are partly right. The gate is old, and the sense it gives is new.

items.p: Match each odd result to its best explanation.
pairs: Reading in a car makes you sick
eyes and inner ears send messages that do not match
You feel dizzy after spinning
the liquid in the canals keeps swirling
A pinched elbow feels better when you rub it
touch signals compete with pain signals
A chilli feels hot
it opens the same gate as heat
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each result has a cause inside the body. The senses are working correctly in all four, and the surprises come from how the messages are mixed or tuned.

items.p: Why is an average of many people more trustworthy than one person's result? Give an example from a balance test.
items.a: One person can have a lucky or unlucky try. An average of many people smooths out luck and shows the pattern most people share. For example, if one child holds 30 seconds on the blanket with eyes shut, that may be a fluke, but the average of eight people shows what is typical.
items.why: Averages help a test show a pattern and not a fluke.

items.p: Why do doctors move a patient's head through a set of positions to treat the spinning caused by loose ear crystals?
opts: To roll the crystals out of the canal and back into their pouch
To make the canals bigger
To stop the eyes flicking
items.why: Loose crystals in a canal push the liquid and make the brain think the head is turning. A doctor can guide them back into the pouch by moving the head in a set order. The canals do not change size.

applications: Doctors test a patient's balance by watching the eyes after the head is turned, or after warm or cool water is put in the ear, a method that goes back to Bárány.
Doctors treat loose ear crystals by moving the head through a set of positions that roll the crystals back into their pouch.
Physiotherapists ask patients to stand with eyes shut or on foam, to find out which of the three balance helpers has weakened after an injury.
Pilots are trained to trust their instruments in cloud, because their inner ears can be fooled when the picture outside is missing.
Handrails and walking sticks that are touched lightly help older people stand steadier, by giving the brain extra information.
Planners design night paths, bathrooms and staircases for older people with low lights, rough strips and firm mats.
Thermostats in refrigerators, geysers, irons and air conditioners use the same loop as the body: sense, compare, act, check.
Clay matkas, wet khus screens and desert coolers keep things cool by letting water dry off a surface and carry heat away.
Gyroscope chips in phones, drones and cameras sense turning with tiny vibrating parts, using the same push that a fly's halteres feel.
Thermal cameras and night-vision cameras sense heat from a distance, as the pits of a snake do.
Nurses and parents use distraction, such as bubbles, songs and stories, to make injections hurt less for children.

open_questions.q: How does the brain mix signals from the eyes, ears and feet into one steady feeling of being upright?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have models of how signals are weighed and combined. Nobody has a full account of how this becomes the plain feeling of standing up.

open_questions.q: Why do some people get travel sickness, and others never?
open_questions.why_open: Two main ideas exist, one about senses that disagree and one about the body struggling to keep steady. Neither explains everything.

open_questions.q: Is pain a sense, or something the brain builds from many clues?
open_questions.why_open: Pain signals can be measured, and pain can change without the signal changing. Scientists disagree about where to draw the line between the signal and the pain.

open_questions.q: How do the brains of pit vipers combine the picture from their eyes with the heat picture from their pits?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that both kinds of signal meet in the same part of the snake's brain. Nobody knows what the snake's combined picture is like.

open_questions.q: Are there senses in the human body that we have not yet found?
open_questions.why_open: The gates for touch and temperature were only found in the last thirty years. Other gates and sensors may be waiting to be discovered.

open_questions.q: Do other animals feel dizzy when they spin?
open_questions.why_open: Many animals show eye flicking after spinning, which suggests that their balance senses are fooled in the same way. Nobody knows what, if anything, that feels like to them.
