maths.problem: In the Balance Team test, one child stood for 30 seconds with eyes open on the floor, and for 6 seconds with eyes shut on the blanket. How many times as long was the first time? What does the number tell you?
maths.answer: 5 times as long. Losing two helpers cut the time to a fifth.
maths.explain: 30 divided by 6 is 5. So the first time was 5 times the second. The result shows how much the eyes and the feet helped the ears.
maths.context: In the Balance Team test, you stand on one foot with and without your eyes, on the floor and on a blanket.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one result by another tells you how many times bigger it is, which is a clearer way to compare tests than just saying one is longer.

maths.problem: A fingertip touch on a wall has a force of 100 grams. A child weighs 25 kilograms. 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams. How many times heavier is the child than the touch?
maths.explain: 25 kilograms is 25 times 1,000, which is 25,000 grams. 25,000 divided by 100 is 250. The child is 250 times heavier than the touch.
maths.context: In A Fingertip Lighter than a Tomato, you steady yourself with a touch lighter than a tomato.
maths.why_maths: Changing kilograms to grams puts the two weights in the same unit, so you can see how tiny the touch is compared with the body it steadies.

maths.problem: Five people stood on one foot with eyes shut for 8, 12, 15, 9 and 6 seconds. What is the average, and why is it more useful than one person's time?
maths.answer: The average is 10 seconds. One person's time can be a fluke.
maths.explain: 8 plus 12 plus 15 plus 9 plus 6 is 50. 50 divided by 5 is 10. An average of five people smooths out luck and shows what is typical.
maths.context: In the Family Balance Lab, you test several people and find the average for each test.
maths.why_maths: An average over several people shows the pattern that most people share, instead of one lucky or unlucky try.

maths.problem: In the Shake the Head or Shake the Page test, a child read 14 of 16 words with her head shaking, and 4 of 16 with the page shaking. What fraction was read right in each case? How many times as many words did she read with the head shaking?
maths.answer: 7 out of 8 with the head shaking, and 1 out of 4 with the page shaking. About 3 and a half times as many.
maths.explain: 14 out of 16 is 7 out of 8, and 4 out of 16 is 1 out of 4. 14 divided by 4 is 3 and a half. So she read about 3 and a half times as many words with her head shaking.
maths.context: In the Shake the Head or Shake the Page test, you count words read right in 10 seconds with the head or the page shaking.
maths.why_maths: Fractions let you compare two scores that come from the same number of words.

maths.problem: In Be a Pit Viper, there are three tumblers and one is warm. Luck would give 4 right answers in 12 rounds. A child got 9 right. How many more than luck is that, and what fraction of the rounds did she get right?
maths.answer: 5 more than luck. She got 3 out of 4 of the rounds right.
maths.explain: 9 minus 4 is 5. 9 out of 12 is 3 out of 4. A score well above luck suggests that she really felt the warmth.
maths.context: In Be a Pit Viper, you try to find the warm tumbler with your eyes shut.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a score with what luck alone would give is how you know whether a result means something.

maths.problem: In Matka Magic, both tumblers started at 39 degrees Celsius. After 15 minutes, the one with the wet cloth was 33.5 degrees and the one with the dry cloth was 36.5 degrees. How much did each cool? How many times as much did the wet one cool?
maths.answer: The wet one cooled by 5.5 degrees and the dry one by 2.5 degrees. The wet one cooled a little over twice as much.
maths.explain: 39 minus 33.5 is 5.5. 39 minus 36.5 is 2.5. 5.5 divided by 2.5 is 2.2. So the wet one cooled about 2.2 times as much.
maths.context: In Matka Magic, you cool warm water with a wet cloth and a dry cloth in front of a fan.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting each start from each finish gives the cooling, and dividing one by the other shows how much better the wet cloth worked.

maths.problem: In Count Your Own Heartbeat, a child felt 38 beats in 30 seconds. Her pulse count for the same time was 40. How many beats a minute is each? What fraction of her pulse count did she feel?
maths.answer: 76 beats a minute by feeling and 80 by pulse. She was 38 out of 40, which is 19 out of 20.
maths.explain: A minute is twice 30 seconds, so 38 times 2 is 76 and 40 times 2 is 80. 38 out of 40 is 19 out of 20, which is 95 out of 100.
maths.context: In Count Your Own Heartbeat, you count your heartbeats by feeling and by pulse.
maths.why_maths: Doubling a 30-second count gives beats in a minute, which is the way doctors and nurses talk about the heart.

maths.problem: In Ice in the Palm, a child rated the ache 7 and 5 when she only watched the ice cube, and 4 and 6 when she counted backwards. What is the average for each kind of try? Is that enough to be sure that counting helps?
maths.answer: Watching averaged 6 and counting averaged 5. It is not enough to be sure.
maths.explain: 7 plus 5 is 12, and 12 divided by 2 is 6. 4 plus 6 is 10, and 10 divided by 2 is 5. The difference of 1 is smaller than the difference between her two watch tries, so more tries would be needed.
maths.context: In Ice in the Palm, you rate the ache from an ice cube while watching and while counting backwards.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the size of a difference with how much the results vary from try to try tells you whether to trust a pattern.

maths.problem: Suppose a fast pain fibre carries a signal at 20 metres a second, and a slow one at 1 metre a second. The path from a toe to the brain is 1.2 metres. How long does each signal take? How much later does the slow signal arrive?
maths.answer: The fast signal takes 0.06 seconds and the slow one 1.2 seconds. The slow one arrives 1.14 seconds later.
maths.explain: Time is distance divided by speed. 1.2 divided by 20 is 0.06. 1.2 divided by 1 is 1.2. The slow signal arrives 1.2 minus 0.06, which is 1.14 seconds later. These speeds are made-up round numbers to show the idea.
maths.context: This is about the two kinds of pain you feel when you stub your toe: a sharp jab first and a throb later.
maths.why_maths: Dividing distance by speed shows why the same hurt can reach the brain at two different times.

roots.context: We have stood on one foot with our eyes open and shut, read while our heads shook and while the page shook, and felt warmth, cold and pain. Now we ask what these senses tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Nothing in you holds you upright by itself. Your eyes, your inner ears and the sensors in your legs each give a rough answer. Your brain mixes the answers, and when one goes missing it listens more to the others.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'my sense of balance' as if it were one organ in the ears, like the eye for seeing. But the ears alone cannot keep you steady. People with damaged inner ears can often stand in the light on a firm floor, and fall in the dark.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Balance Team test, standing on a blanket with eyes shut took away sight and made the feet unsure. Only the ears were left clear, and the standing time was usually the shortest. If your own results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: You feel one thing: 'I am upright'. You do not feel your eyes, inner ears and legs reporting one by one, because your brain builds that one feeling from all of them at once.
three.what_is_life: A fly steers with two tiny clubs, a python hunts by heat, and a fish balances with stones in her ears. Each living being has the senses that suit the life they live.
three.what_is_this_world: Down is real, but nobody feels it directly. A fish and a child each find down in a different way, by stones or by crystals, and a fly feels its turning with clubs. The same world pushes on all of them.

roots.thread: Gravity pulls on everything, and turning pushes on everything. A crystal in your ear, a stone in a fish's ear and a swinging club in a fly are all small things that gravity or turning pushes, and a nerve feels the push. Your eyes add what they see, and your feet add what the ground feels like. The brain joins all of these into one feeling. A body stays upright by noticing the pushes and pulls of the world and correcting for them, again and again.

teachings.teaching: A person is born gentle and soft, and dies hard and stiff. Plants are tender and full of sap when alive, and dry and brittle when dead. So the stiff and unbending are companions of death, and the gentle and yielding are companions of life. A tree that will not bend is easily broken.
teachings.link: A standing body is never still. It sways a little and corrects, again and again. A body that stiffens up corrects less well, and balance depends on that give and take.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha reminded Sona, a lute player who was trying too hard, that a lute makes music only when its strings are neither too tight nor too loose. Effort needs the same even tuning.
teachings.link: Balance is a kind of tuning. The brain keeps adjusting how much it trusts each helper, neither too much nor too little, and the muscles adjust again and again.

science.text: The canals of the inner ear sense turning, the ear crystals sense tilting and speeding up, and the brain combines them with sight and the body's own sensors.

The brain may weigh each source of information by how reliable it is, trusting a steady one more than a noisy one. Tests with sight and touch fit this idea, and it is one of the main ideas in brain science today.
How these mixed signals become the plain feeling of being upright is not known.

other_view.view: Staying upright is only a feedback loop: sensors measure, a rule decides, and muscles act. Words like team, vote or agreement are just ways of picturing it. The science needs only the signals and the rule.

how_we_found_out.story: Many people once assumed that the three loops in the inner ear were part of hearing, because they sit right beside the part that hears. In the 1820s, the French scientist Pierre Flourens cut the loops in pigeons. The pigeons could still hear, but they tumbled and swung their heads wildly. So the loops had another job. Still, nobody knew how doctors could test them. About 1906 in Vienna, a young doctor named Robert Bárány was washing a patient's ears with water. When the water was cooler than the body, the patient's eyes flicked one way and the patient felt dizzy. When it was warmer, the eyes flicked the other way. Bárány worked out that the water was warming or cooling the liquid in the loop and making it flow, just as a spinning head would. For the first time, doctors could test each ear alone. In 1914 he won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
how_we_found_out.who: Pierre Flourens, a French scientist (1794 to 1867), and Robert Bárány, an Austro-Hungarian doctor (1876 to 1936)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The idea that the loops of the inner ear were part of hearing. Flourens showed that pigeons without the loops could hear but could not stay upright.
